News.title: Asylum seekers encouraged to move in with friends & family in latest Home office booklet after ‘don’t rape’ leaflet
News.content:
ASYLUM seekers are being encouraged to move out of Home Office accommodation and stay with friends and family, The Sun can reveal.

A booklet handed out to new arrivals suggests they consider the move — and offers to cover travel costs.



But it raises fears that asylum seekers “can simply disappear” unless the system for monitoring their whereabouts is improved.

The Sun revealed on Thursday how another pamphlet in the series warned migrants not to rape.



The latest one reads: “You can stay with friends or family instead of in Home Office accommodation.

“It will not impact the outcome of your asylum application, and if eligible, you will still get weekly money for food and other essential items.”



The Home Office is under scrutiny over plans to move asylum seekers out of expensive hotels into old military camps — which can be even more costly.

As an incentive to leave its sites, the leaflet says: “We may be able to help with travel costs to your new accommodation.”

Sussex Police and Crime Commissioner Katy Bourne said the leaflet raises questions about how asylum seekers will be found once they leave Home Office sites.

She said: “The Home Office admits it has no mechanism for finding them, which is shocking.



“Unless we have a better system of monitoring their movements, they can simply disappear.”

Figures show 93,653 people are in taxpayer-funded asylum accommodation, including 20,885 in hotels.

Another 3,866 asylum seekers are receiving only subsistence support — meaning they have sourced their own housing — which is up 25 per cent in a year.

Asylum seekers can receive £49.18 a week to cover essentials such as food and toiletries while their claims are processed, but they cannot usually work.

Other booklets offered to new arrivals give advice on UK laws, such as telling them rape is illegal and the age of consent is 16.



PM Andy Burnham defended the leaflets, saying: “If you break UK law, you will be removed from the country.

“So it follows if we’re taking this approach, it’s made clear what the UK law is.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “There’s been no change and Home Office accommodation continues to be provided only to those asylum seekers who have nowhere else to stay.

“We’ve cut costs by £1 billion since the general election and are determined to reduce the bill further.”

News.title: Hilarious moment Amazon delivery drone drops package directly into swimming pool as customer is left fuming
News.content:
THIS is the hilarious moment a delivery drone opens its hatch – and dumps its Amazon package directly into a swimming pool.

Lindsey Austen, from Texas, heard a loud buzzing sound and ran into her garden – only to be met with an astonishing sight.



Bizarre footage filmed by Lindsey shows the high-tech bot from Amazon’s Prime Air swooping into her back yard.

Bristling with six mini propellers, the drone artfully hovers over the pool – before suddenly unloading its contents from a height of around 30ft.



The cardboard box lands with a splash and can be seen bobbing in the water as the bot buzzes away.

“When it went into the pool, I was shocked,” Lindsey said, adding: “I don’t think I’ll be wanting any more drone deliveries.”

Shared by ABC7 News on Wednesday, the clip has since been seen thousands of times.

One viewer joked: “I love how it gently drops my package from over 30 feet in the air. Now that’s proper care.”

“Maybe she ordered a pool float”, another quipped.

The tech giant previously stressed that its drones deliver packages safely and quietly.



“Once the drone arrives at the preferred delivery point with a customer’s order, it will check to confirm there are no people, pets, or vehicles in the way before safely delivering the package”, said a spokesperson for Amazon.

It comes after another drone mishap in May where a bot dropped a package next to a pond where the force of landing sent it flying into the water.

Last year an Amazon delivery drone plopped a package next to a pool in Arizona – but the gusts of wind from the bot’s propellers blew the box into the water.



Amazon’s Prime Air service is still in its early phases – but the mega corp recently announced plans to expand to 500 new cities.

Some residents have already raised concerns about the disruptive sound of the delivery bots.

One Facebook user said: “Saw one just now outside my home. They’re louder than I was thinking they would be.”

Another commented: “I saw one yesterday flying over my neighborhood. It sounded like a small plane.”

Amazon has brushed off their complaints and said the sound level is comparable to an electric toothbrush.

News.title: Shocking moment small boat migrants on French beach attack cops as they try to set sail to Britain
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment boat migrants attacked French cops as they tried to set sail for Britain.

The lifejacket-wearing group can be seen appearing to hurl objects at officers as police move in on their inflatable dinghy in Northern France.



Cops respond with Pava spray before slashing the boat with a knife to stop it launching across the Channel.

Footage of the incident was released by the Home Office and shows a group of migrants running down a beach with a dinghy, headed for the sea.



A French police vehicle can be seen racing to stop them from launching the craft, pulling up in front of the group of migrants.

Cops pile out of their cars and rush to stop the launch from going ahead – as the migrants fight back in shocking scenes.



An officer can be seen approaching the dinghy and slashing it twice to deflate it.

The footage was released as new figures were published on efforts to stop migrants making the journey to Britain.



French units prevented 185 “small boat crossing events” between April 27 and August 2, according to data supplied by French authorities.

That included stopping launches, seizing boats and engines and arresting suspected people smugglers.

Officials claim the action prevented more than 4,300 migrants from attempting to reach British shores over the three months.

But thousands are still making it across the Channel.



Some 15,897 migrants have reached Britain by small boat so far this year – although that is down 43 per cent on the same point last year.

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp branded the fresh figures a “joke.”

He added that: “Channel crossings preventions are down by half over the past year and, as we exposed earlier this month, French police are under instruction not to intervene when immigrants are attempting to cross.

“The only way we can stop the crossings is by having a proper deterrent. If people know they can stay in the UK, get put up in a hotel and claim benefits then they will keep risking these dangerous journeys.”



Smuggling gangs also appear have switched tactics by cramming increasing numbers of migrants into individual dinghies.

Earlier this month, a record 230 people made the journey in a single boat.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

French authorities also revealed just 40 illegal migrants have been deported since a separate detention trial began on May 1.

Some 119 migrants have been detained under the scheme, with 76 still being held and 32 released.

News.title: Daniel Kinahan-linked Scots beauty firm being forced to shut down
News.content:
A SCOTS cosmetics firm linked to suspected Irish crime boss Daniel Kinahan is being forced into closure.

Global Beauty Enterprises Ltd — run by associate Sandra McClumpha, 57, — is being liquidated by court order.





Companies House records show the Glasgow-based outfit had been subject to several compulsory strike-off notices over the previous year.

McClumpha and her Irish business associate Ronan Cruise, 60, are directors.

Its looming demise comes as Kinahan, 49, is facing trial in Dublin charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

He has been remanded in custody since being extradited from Dubai to Ireland earlier this month.

McClumpha was a director of Kinahan-linked boxing business Global Promotions Management, formerly called MTK Global.

We told how she was pictured with him weeks before a £3.7million bounty was put on him as part of a global manhunt four years ago.

McClumpha, of Uddingston, near Glasgow, posed for the photo with the alleged crimelord as they met a senior Pakistani politician in Dubai.

The US Department of State announced the huge reward for information leading to the financial disruption or arrest and/or conviction of Kinahan plus his dad Christy Sr, 69, and brother Christy Jr, 45.





Officials alleged he headed a “narco-terrorist” group.

McClumpha quit as chief executive officer of MTK Global in 2020.

Official filings show she has held directorship with 15 firms, including the now-dissolved Fake Bake UK Ltd — a previous sponsor of MTK boxing events.

She remains a director of Global Beauty Enterprises plus WBR Global, previously named Browncow Tanning.

Daniel Kinahan was flown to Ireland on an Irish Government jet on Sunday, August 9 and immediately taken by high-speed Garda escort to court in Dublin.

He was charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

With no legal representation, the Dublin man was remanded into custody and transferred to the maximum-security Portlaoise Prison in the Irish midlands.

Kinahan was brought to Portlaoise by Gardai who drove in a convoy of BMWs and was admitted to the A-block.



Some of the most high-profile residents in the prison and others facing trial at the Special Criminal Court are housed in the wing.

The cell was “refreshed” according to sources, cleaned and given a fresh lick of paint.

Kinahan, alleged to be a leader of the Kinahan organised crime group, was arrested in the United Arab Emirates on April 15 on foot of an arrest warrant issued by the Irish courts.

This was carried out in accordance with a bilateral agreement on extradition between Ireland and the UAE.

The Irish Sun previously revealed that the Kinahan cartel still has “significant people” operating across Ireland.

The narco terrorist group’s “principal representative” Ross Browning, 48, remains in the country, but the transnational crime gang no longer has complete control of the entire drugs market.

Investigators from the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau believe the Kinahan Organised Crime Group’s leadership in Dubai are working with criminal gangs across Europe to control cocaine supply routes from South America to the continent.

And the Gardai believe the Kinahan network is now operating a “franchise business” focusing on the drug wholesale and importation role.

Many of the Kinahan associates are no longer part of “cell structures” and are no longer taking orders from their HQ in Dubai.

The tight control structures are now regarded by Gardai as “fractured and loose.”

News.title: Hero neighbour in pyjamas battled house blaze with jet washer before woman tragically died as cops probe murder
News.content:
A HERO neighbour in his pyjamas battled a house blaze that killed a woman, as cops probe a suspected murder.

The 48-year-old woman died and eight others were injured in the house fire that tore through a home on Berkley Avenue, Hounslow, West London, just after 1am on Wednesday.



Armed with a jet washer, shopkeeper Satwant Singh, 48, rushed outside to fight the fire while still in his pyjamas.

His daughter had spotted the fire from her bedroom window and woken him up in the middle of the night.



He told The Sun: “I told my wife to get all the children outside and then opened up the alleyway side door and brought the jet wash around the front of the house to spray the fire.

“I could see that the door was on fire but there was smoke everywhere else.

Satwant said he put out “most of the fire”, adding: “I didn’t think about myself, I was just thinking that I needed to help.

“We are Sikhs. My culture says we should help people. It doesn’t matter who you are.”

His wife Barkash, praised his bravery and said she begged him to move from the flames, but that he continued spraying the house.



She said: “He is very brave. I think the water from the jet wash reduced the smoke coming from the house and helped people get out.”

She added: “When we went outside we saw a man who lived in the house on the roof shouting for people to get out.”



Barkash said the fire had calmed down when the fire brigade arrived.

The mum-of-three realised the house next door was on fire when her 14-year-old daughter Jennica rushed into her bedroom.

Jennica said: “I was woken up by a bang and when I looked outside I saw the reflection of fire in the car.”

After the fire, the family couldn’t sleep, Barkash said.

She added: “I can’t forget the sound of people shouting ‘help, help’, neighbours saying to move the vehicles and the man on the roof shouting for people to leave the house. We were so panicked.”



Shaf Akmal, 40, said he was one of the first people outside.

He said: “I saw two men who stood on the back of a car parked in the driveway of the house and broke the downstairs window to pull two people out.”

Shaf’s ring doorbell footage showed the house suddenly being engulfed in flames.

Officers attended the scene alongside the London Fire Brigade and London Ambulance Service.

Nine people were taken to hospital as a result of their injuries, where one woman died.



A murder investigation has since been launched but no arrests have been made so far.

Detective Chief Inspector Neil John, who is leading the investigation, said:

“Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim’s family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time, as well as everyone who has been injured.

“Our enquiries are progressing at pace as we work to establish the full circumstances surrounding the fire, which we believe may have been started deliberately.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We understand this to be an isolated incident within a residential address; however, we understand it will cause concern within the local community.”



They urged anyone with information, or footage that may assist the investigation, to contact police.

News.title: British Airways cabin boss ‘sexually assaulted sleeping air hostess at his home after drinking with her at a dinner’
News.content:
BA CREW 'PREYED ON' British Airways cabin boss ‘sexually assaulted sleeping air hostess at his home after drinking with her at a dinner’

A BRITISH Airways cabin boss preyed on a sleeping air hostess after downing beer and wine at his home, a court heard.

Amardip “Amo” Dhariwal, 55, allegedly assaulted the female colleague after boozing with her over dinner.



The ex-lead flight manager is on trial for a single attack on one woman in 2022 — but a jury has heard from two other stewardesses who alleged he raped them on foreign trips.

Dhariwal denies one count of sexual assault by penetration. Reading crown court heard he invited the woman to his then-home in Bracknell, Berks, for dinner, where they drank beer and wine.



The woman, then engaged and now married, said she dozed off as they watched a film and woke to find Dhariwal touching her intimately.

Prosecutor James Partridge told jurors: “They met three months prior to the incident on a flight to Cape Town.

“They got on so well that they met for coffee a few times. She went to his house for taco and movie nights.”

She even referred to Dhariwal as her “work husband”.

Mr Partridge added: “They started watching a film. As they watched it, the victim said she had her legs up.

“She awoke to the defendant touching her.”



He said the woman “felt bewildered” and escaped by finding a key while he was upstairs and called a friend “crying and whispering” on the phone.

Dhariwal, now of Southall, West London, told police: “Anything that happened was consensual.”

The jury was told Dhariwal allegedly raped a colleague in a Singapore hotel room in 2020. She woke naked in his bed, confused by how she got there, she said.

Local police investigated but took no further action and would not help British cops, it was said.

The other stewardess claimed she was assaulted while asleep and drunk in a hotel room in Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur in 2018.



The trial continues.

News.title: Bizarre moment Putin peers at bones of 650-year-old warrior ‘set to be worshipped by Russian soldiers fighting Ukraine’
News.content:
THIS is the bizarre moment Vladimir Putin takes a break from waging war on Ukraine to peer at the bones of a 650-year-old saint.

The ageing dictator has landed on a new tactic to boost morale – sending his soldiers a medieval corpse.



The body of Dmitry Donskoy, who died in 1389, was uncovered during restoration work at Moscow’s Cathedral of the Archangel.

Famous for fighting the Mongols on the Don river in 1380, the medieval warrior prince was sainted in 1988.



Now Donskoy may enter a warzone once again – with bits of his bones dispatched to the frontline.

Bizarre footage shows the tyrant crossing himself as he bends down to gaze at the desiccated corpse – before lighting a candle in prayer.



The despot rarely visits the frontline – instead cowering in his bunker with more than 800 elite security guards watching his every move.

In the absence of their tyrannical ruler, soldiers will now be able to worship some saintly bones in the midst of deadly drone warfare.

Church official Vakhtang Kipshidze said: “Everyone shares the opinion that the opportunity for such veneration should be provided to Orthodox military personnel as soon as possible.”

Putin has given the plan his go ahead and “best wishes”.



“Even the relics are going to war, but Putin isn’t” taunted Ukrainian news channel Pravda Gerashchenko.

Bits of the skeleton are set to be shipped to the frontline – where some officials believe they can lend “spiritual support”.

The move has also been mocked online, with one commenter posting on X: “Nothing says better about encouraging your troops in a battlefield by parading the corpse of a dead guy.”



Combat wounds can be spotted on his skeleton – though the ruler died of natural causes aged 39.

Just last month, the Russian army lost the bones of Prince Alexander Nevsky.

The relic was being transported for a prayer service against the spiralling fuel crisis.

But the convoy came under attack on the road – and authorities admitted that the shrine had been “completely lost”.

Three Russian soldiers also died in the drone blasts.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Putin does not often visit his ailing armies – and in May was gripped by assassination fears, banning his staff from taking the bus or using mobile phones.

The Russian tyrant, once the world’s ultimate tough guy, went into total meltdown, according to a report from The Financial Times.

News.title: Prince Harry's return reason 'revealed' as Meghan Markle 'offered huge UK role'
News.content:
Prince Harry's return reason 'revealed' as Meghan Markle 'offered huge UK role'

The reason behind the Duke and Duchess' impending move back to the UK from California in the US is reportedly centred around a career opportunity for Meghan Markle

View 4 Images Meghan and Harry's move back to the UK is reportedly based on a job opportunity for the Duchess of Sussex (Image: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP)

The real reason Meghan Markle and Prince Harry are set to return to the UK has reportedly been revealed - less than a day after the shock move was announced.

‌



It was revealed on Wednesday that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex will be returning home this September, and that they had enrolled their children Archie and Lilibet Mountbatten-Windsor in a British school. The move was communicated to King Charles III only on Sunday, it is understood, and until now there was no indication as to what it had been predicated by.

‌



It has now been reported that the reason behind the decision came after Meghan received an offer for a role in an upcoming British-based project.

‌



The signs Prince Harry has been plotting his and Meghan’s return to the UK READ MORE :

View 4 Images Meghan and Harry are returning to the UK with their children (Image: Meghan/Instagram)

News.com.au reports, citing entertainment sources, that the Duchess has been offered an undisclosed role in the upcoming project. Further details are yet to be shared about the position, and follows news that the couple are expected to remain financially independent and continue their commercial and charitable work.

Harry is not expected to undertake official royal duties. They are retaining their home in Montecito, California as well as their holiday home in Portugal.

‌



The King, who is still living with cancer, was first made aware of the move on Sunday, only three days before it was made public, but is understood to welcome the opportunity to see more of the family both in a private and personal capacity.

View 4 Images Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK (Image: Getty Images)

However, the decision is particularly striking given Harry's previous concerns about bringing his family back to Britain as he does not automatically get taxpayer-funded security while in the UK.

‌



The Duke has spent years challenging the decision in the courts over his security arrangements after losing the protection when he ceased to be a working royal and moved overseas.

The Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), an independent body overseen by the Home Office that makes security arrangements for the Royal Family and other high-profile individuals, has previously decided while the two were not permanently living in the UK that their arrangements would be made on a case-by-case basis.

View 4 Images Meghan Markle has reportedly been offered a new job in the UK (Image: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire)

‌



Their security arrangements will be a "private matter" Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement on Thursday. He has no role in making security decisions for the royals.

He said: "It's a matter for Harry and for Meghan, and we wish them well in the move that they are making." The Home Office would not comment on the specifics of high-profile arrangements, telling the BBC in a statement that it was "long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals' security".

It did say, however, that the UK's protective security system was rigorous and proportionate. The couple's security arrangements became a point of contention after the couple left the country and stepped back from their royal duties in 2020.

Article continues below

The two settled in Montecito, California with Archie, who was born in the UK, and welcomed their second child, Lilibet, some years later in 2021. During their time stateside they have employed a private security team.

News.title: Cries of 'yes' as NHS worker who made £200K from dodgy fire sticks avoid prison
News.content:
Cries of 'yes' as NHS worker who made £200K from dodgy fire sticks avoid prison

NHS worker Craig Austin, 38, supplied more than 1,000 people with illegal access to Sky and BT Sports streams in a secret side hustle which earned him more than £200,000

View 3 Images Craig Austin made more than £200k selling 'dodgy fire sticks' (Image: Liverpool Echo)

An NHS worker secretly built a £200,000-plus side hustle selling 'dodgy fire sticks' to more than 1,000 customers, a court heard.

‌



Craig Austin, 38, spent around five years supplying illegal IPTV subscriptions which gave customers access to Sky Sports and BT Sports, now TNT Sports.

‌



The former ambulance service employee promoted the services through social media while, he told police, trying to "make ends meet" after his wife lost her job.

‌



But the scale of the business was laid bare at Liverpool Crown Court, where prosecutors said 1,116 users had been identified and Austin had received £205,700.72 in payments. As he was spared jail, cries of "yes" were heard from his supporters in court, Liverpool Echo reports.

An anti-piracy investigator from Sky estimated that Austin's activities could have potentially cost the broadcaster more than £3.5 million.

The 38-year-old was identified as the operator of an X account called 'Aussie 90' which advertised "dodgy fire sticks". His account came to the attention of Merseyside Police and FACT after test purchases were made in March 2023 and May 2025.

‌



View 3 Images Craig Austin outside Liverpool Crown Court (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Burned bodies of lawyers found embracing in cockpit after hunt for missing plane READ MORE :

Detectives subsequently examined Austin's PayPal and bank accounts, uncovering customer payments dating back to January 2020.

Police later raided his home in Whiston on August 7 last year, seizing mobile phones and fire sticks.

‌



Olivia Belle, prosecuting, described how Austin would offer six month subscriptions for Sky Sports and BT Sports streams via IPTV for £40, or £80 for 12 months.

During his police interview, the defendant told officers he had stopped the operation the previous June after he "realised that people were being prosecuted". He also admitted he "knew it was dodgy" but was doing it to make ends meet after his wife lost her job.

A judge told Austin as he was spared prison today: "This is really serious behaviour. The figures involved are eye-watering."

‌



Austin, who has no previous convictions, has two young children.

Nicola Daley, defending, told the court that his remorse and efforts to rebuild his life should be taken into account.

She said: "In my submission, although this is, on the one hand, serious offending, that is outweighed on the balancing scales by the significant mitigation. In my submission, his genuine remorse feeds into the realistic prospect of rehabilitation.

‌



"The author of that probation report has noted positive admissions. There is still work that can be done.

"This is somebody who, despite losing his good name and losing his work for the NHS, not significantly well paid, but still work he had done for a number of years, he has gone out and found himself another job.

"I can assure the court that he does take his responsibility seriously. He has come to court today expecting the potential of receiving a custodial sentence."

‌



View 3 Images The case was heard at Liverpool Crown Court (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Austin admitted three counts of making or supplying an article for use in fraud and acquiring criminal property.

He was handed a 32-month sentence suspended for three years with 150 hours of unpaid work and a rehabilitation activity requirement of up to 20 days.

‌



Sentencing, Recorder Daniel Lister said he was satisfied Austin had demonstrated remorse after engaging in "five years worth of serious dishonesty".

The judge added: "It is clear that you are not only someone with another side to you, because you are a caring and attentive father and husband, but you have also worked in a responsible role with the ambulance service and conducted yourself in that role in a way that would be commendable."

Mr Lister said there is a "level of sophistication" in the nature of Austin's offending but that he was sure the dad is "very unlikely to be involved with the criminal justice system in this way again."

‌



The judge continued: "The mitigation in this case is your lack of previous convictions, your remorse, your positive good character, the personal circumstances that have been set out to me in the way that you support your wife and children and that you have prospects of work in the future.

"In this case, I am satisfied that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community.

"You do not present a high risk of reoffending. You have strong personal mitigation. It is clear that you have children who are dependant upon you, and there would be an impact on them if you were imprisoned.

Article continues below

"This is really serious behaviour. You are fortunate to find yourself in a situation where prisons are full and, frankly, someone like you who has not been in trouble before can be dealt with in the community.

"That does not mean this offending is not very serious indeed. The figures involved are eye-watering."

News.title: Peru struck by 6.7-mag earthquake felt in Ayacucho and Ica, causing landslides
News.content:
Peru struck by 6.7-mag earthquake felt in Ayacucho and Ica, causing landslides

A magnitude 6.7 earthquake hit Peru earlier today and caused landslides in the southern Andes Mountains - it was felt in several regions including Ayacucho, Ica and Arequipa

View Image The earthquake was centred 38km (24 miles) northwest of the city of Upahuacho (Image: US Geological Survey (USGS))

A magnitude 6.7 earthquake shook Peru's southern Andes Mountains on Thursday.

‌



According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the quake occurred at 1pm local time (6pm UK time) and was centred 38km (24 miles) northwest of the city of Upahuacho, in the Parinacochas province of the Ayacucho region.

‌



There were no immediate reports of damage or injuries, and no tsunami warning has been issued.

‌



However, the quake has reportedly led to landslides in the area, with footage shared on social media showing locals in the streets looking up at debris falling down nearby mountainsides.

The earthquake had a depth of 66.7km and was felt in several regions of southern Peru, including Ica and Arequipa.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Earthquakes are frequent in Peru which is part of the Pacific "Ring of Fire", an area of frequent seismic activity.

In 2007, a magnitude 7.9 earthquake in a province of the Ica region left nearly 600 people dead.

It follows a major 7.4-mag earthquake in Colombia earlier this month which led to hundreds of deaths.

‌



President Abelardo de la Espriella has asked Donald Trump to suspend tariffs to help Colombia recover from the earthquake, which killed at least 289 people.

De la Espriella took office just days before the quake struck. He was backed by Trump in Colombia's closely contested presidential election, which was decided in a runoff on June 21, and has sought to emphasise his connections with the US leader.

On Saturday night, de la Espriella wrote on X that he spoke with Trump and thanked him for aid sent by the US in response to the earthquake.

Article continues below

He added that he "asked him to consider the temporary suspension of the high tariffs that affect Colombian products, in order to provide relief to our businesspeople, who are facing very difficult times due to the effects of the earthquake".

News.title: 'Do not swim' warning at three UK beaches over 'contaminated water' fears
News.content:
'Do not swim' warning at three UK beaches over 'contaminated water' fears

Three beaches on the Isle of Wight have been closed to swimmers after rainfall resulted in 'outfall release that may have affected water quality', the Environment Agency warned

View Image The warning covers beaches at Gurnard, Isle of Wight (file) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Swimmers have been warned to stay out of the sea at three popular UK beaches after rainfall triggered an "outfall release", sparking fears of contaminated water.

‌



An alert has been issued by the Environment Agency for parts of the Isle of Wight following "an outfall release within the last 24 hours which may have affected water quality".

‌



The warning covers beaches at Gurnard on the island's northern coast, as well as Shanklin and Bembridge to the east.

‌



The Environment Agency is urging people not to enter the water in the affected areas, while the Isle of Wight Council has urged visitors "not to come into direct contact with contaminated water".

The council warned that sewage water " can contain bacteria and viruses that may cause illness".

UK weather maps shows 30C in 7 counties next week after Met Office 'hot' forecast READ MORE :

Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Friday with downpours in 10 counties READ MORE :

Anyone who does come into contact with the water should " wash with soap and water" as hand sanitizer "does not kill all viruses which can cause illness".

‌



Signs warning the public have been installed at the affected beaches, with a council spokesperson saying it had taken " immediate action to support public awareness and safety".

Details of the warning have also been shared online by the council and through Southern Water's River and Seas Watch website.

The alert has left some members of the public fuming, with one person describing the situation as an "utter disgrace".

‌



One person commented: "This is disgusting. It cannot be from 'storm' drains."

A Facebook user added: " So so gross. Why is nothing being done about this!!?"

It comes after a number of pollution-related warnings have been issued around the Isle of Wight's coastline this summer.

Article continues below

Anyone requiring more information about the current warning can contact Environment Health on 01983823000.

News.title: Leaders 21/08/26
News.content:
Leaders 21/08/26

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Harry and Meghan may be returning to Britain, but six years of bitterness, accusations and family hurt cannot simply be left behind at the airport. Their departure from royal life caused deep wounds. Harry’s attacks on William, Kate, Charles and Camilla were intensely personal, and relations with his brother in particular have been left in ruins. That is why this homecoming matters. There will be no return to royal duties and no half-in, half-out deal. That has already been decided. What remains unresolved is the family. William has every reason to be wary, and trust will not be restored overnight. The British public, whose affection for the Sussexes has also fallen sharply, may prove equally difficult to win back. But living in Britain again creates an opportunity that distance never could. Harry and Meghan now have the chance to stop the sniping, rebuild bridges and put family before old grievances.

‌



For their children, the King and everyone caught in this miserable feud, they should seize it. Few things show the brilliance of our NHS more clearly than giving a donated organ a second chance to save a life. Doctors have now carried out the first lung transplant under a pioneering scheme which can revive and test organs that might once have been discarded. By pumping lungs with oxygenated blood and nutrients, medics can assess whether they are strong enough for transplant. The breakthrough could increase the number of usable donor lungs by 20 per cent and save or improve 750 more lives every year. Britain is the first country in the world to run a national programme of this kind. That is something worth celebrating. It combines cutting-edge science with the skill and dedication of NHS staff to give desperately ill patients the greatest gift of all: more time.

Sir Rod Stewart has spent decades getting crowds on their feet. This week, Celtic returned the favour. The 81-year-old was all smiles watching his beloved team cruise to victory, just days after undergoing heart surgery. We hope the enforced break does him good and that he is back rocking again soon.

News.title: Lufthansa flight to US declares mid-air emergency at 33,000ft above UK
News.content:
Lufthansa flight to US declares mid-air emergency at 33,000ft above UK

Lufthansa flight LH430 to Chicago diverted to Glasgow after declaring an emergency over Scotland due to a medical incident on board earlier today

View 2 Images A Lufthansa Boeing 747 declared an emergency above the UK today (stock) (Image: Mondadori Portfolio via Getty Images)

A Lufthansa flight to the United States declared an emergency while cruising at around 33,000ft above the UK before diverting to Glasgow.

‌



Flight LH430 had left Frankfurt Airport at midday UK time on Thursday and was heading for Chicago O’Hare International Airport when the aircraft turned back while flying over Scotland.

‌



Around two hours into the nine-hour journey, the Boeing 747-8 made a sharp U-turn while cruising at around 33,000ft before the crew transmitted squawk code 7700, the international aviation code used to signal an emergency.

‌



The aircraft initially appeared to be heading towards Dublin Airport before its diversion changed to Glasgow, where it descended and held at around 10,000ft.

View 2 Images The plane was forced to divert to Glasgow (Image: AirNav Radar)

Article continues below

Jet2 pilot's four chilling words to passengers as flight declares emergency over UK READ MORE :

Ryanair flight declares mid-air emergency after taking off from Birmingham READ MORE :

It eventually landed on runway 05 at 1.24pm local time, around three hours and 21 minutes after take-off.

The aircraft was then parked on a remote stand at Glasgow Airport, with the diversion understood to have been caused by a medical emergency on board.

The plane was refuelled before departing Glasgow at around 5.55pm on Thursday to resume its journey to Chicago.

News.title: Harry and Meghan revealed UK return to security services weeks before telling King
News.content:
Harry and Meghan revealed UK return to security services weeks before telling King

EXCLUSIVE: The royal informed mandarins about the shock move earlier this month in order for them to prepare security measures. His father only found out on Sunday

View 7 Images Harry appeared at an event to support veterans in Washington on Wednesday (Image: AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

Prince Harry told the security services about his impending return to the UK before he told the King, the Mirror can reveal.

‌



The royal informed mandarins about the shock move earlier this month in order for them to prepare security measures. His father only found out on Sunday.

‌



The government are now under pressure to give tax-payer funded protection to the prince, his wife Meghan and their children, when they move to the UK later this month. Harry has been waiting for the Royal and VIP Executive Committee, known as RAVEC, to make a decision about his family’s security arrangements for the last nine months.

‌



View 7 Images Meghan previously shared clips of Archie and Lilibet alongside her and Harry (Image: @meghan/Instagram)

It is understood it has been delayed by a lack of resources, with nine former Prime Ministers and members of the royal family already receiving protection. But the Royal Family's former head of protection Dai Davies says it must now be done urgently as he believes the Sussex's decision to move back to the UK has changed the landscape.

Mr Davies told the Mirror: "The whole risk assessment will have to be reviewed. I wonder, given the short notice, has anybody worked it out for them, because even me, who has been very opposed to him getting protection as a non-royal, now I think the whole scenario is changing.

‌



"He's going to stay in a settled address. His address is going to be known, and obviously the issue regarding his children and going to school is going to be another area where you've got to look at the whole issue of security."

The furore comes as Harry prepares to learn how much he and others, including Elton John and Doreen Lawrence, will have to pay in costs after losing their case against Associated Newspapers on Friday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Harry and Meghan's security arrangements are a "private matter". Speaking on Thursday, Mr Burnham added: "It's a matter for Harry and for Meghan, and we wish them well in the move that they are making."

‌



Harry and Meghan previously lost their right to automatic, taxpayer-funded round-the-clock police security in February 2020 after stepping down as senior working members of the British royal family and moving to the US. Harry later lost a case at the High Court in February 2025 which concluded RAVEC, an independent body overseen by the Home Office, was right to downgrade his high-level police protection when he is back in the country.

View 7 Images Dai Davies was head of Scotland Yard’s Royal Protection Command from 1994 to 1998 (Image: Daily Record)

In May 2025, Harry took his case to the Court of Appeal, but after a two day hearing Judge Sir Geoffrey Vos told the court while the duke’s safety concerns were both “powerful and moving”, his “sense of grievance” did not “translate into a legal argument”. In December, Harry won a new Government review, which is yet to be carried out.

‌



The Home Office has always maintained that Harry’s security is considered on a case-by-case basis, with him required to inform the department of his travel plans at least 28 days in advance. Speaking about the cost and scale of the security now needed to protect the Sussex's, including their children Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, Mr Davies said: "In terms of cost, it's going to cost a huge amount.

"If they've found a premises, that's got to be brought up to date in terms of security and I know how expensive that can be. It's not just securing the windows and doors - it's the technical things, the safe room that has to go in and so on, and then you've got vehicles. An armoured car comes in at about half a million pounds for the top end.

"If they spread each other four ways, with two different schools, and Meghan and him getting it, it's going to cost you and I a huge amount of money. The cost of protecting a family of four now, their home visits, where they're going, their quasi-royal events, the whole thing is gonna cost millions if we have to pay for it, so something has to be decided by somebody with the current up-to-date knowledge and information."

‌



Mr Davies added: "Do we, as tax-payers, actually pick it up? I don't know at this stage. That will be a decision for RAVEC based on the intelligence and information that they will hopefully now get."

View 7 Images Meghan and her children Archie and Lilibet have spent little time in the UK since they were born (Image: meghan/instagram)

Mr Davies believes the issue is a problem for officials, who have to balance spiralling costs and a lack of resources while also ensuring the safety of Harry, who wrote in his autobiography about killing killed 25 Taliban soldiers while serving with the British army.

‌



In 2022, former Met Police Assistant Commissioner Neil Basu told how Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, had faced "disgusting" and "very real" threats to her life. And in May a man was charged after allegedly threatening Harry's uncle Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, previously known as Prince Andrew, during an incident near his home on the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk.

Mr Davies said: "The problem is that Harry is no longer a working Royal and no other non-working royal gets protection. But he can say 'I'm unique', which he is, because of his war service and because of his big mouth and the book he's written. So there are all manner of things that would have to be now taken into consideration.

"There have been in the past attacks on Harry, when he was much younger, and people have gone to prison for it. The whole issue now is up for grabs."

‌



Under the current guidelines for Harry, where intelligence indicates a specific threat or where events require it, local police can provide support or specialist assistance. However, this falls well short of the round-the-clock armed Metropolitan Police protection afforded to working royals.

View 7 Images Harry and Meghan previously lost their right to automatic, taxpayer-funded round-the-clock police security in February 2020 after stepping down as senior working members of the British royal family and moving to the US (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Mr Davies believes police officers will be essential in protecting Harry and his family once they move to the UK. He said: "Common sense would say that that's sensible given the notoriety of the pair of them. The local constabulary and their support structure is so important to the protection and this will have to happen again wherever this house is. The local police clearly will have a response capability. They should be part of the planning in conjunction with his team and all royalty protection, if they're called on to give advice."

‌



Asked about what security will be needed at Archie and Lilibet's school, he said: "If you recall, at different times, William and Harry both had people like [royal protection officer] Ken Wharfe there at that time. They would go to the school and they would have officers based at the school ready to respond.

"Clearly that's another area where you would have to carry out a proper review structure, look at the security, look at how people can get in and out, look at a contingency plan if anybody got in. It's a huge measure and there are issues that would have to be carefully considered."

Mr Davies added: "In my day it was the IRA, or the provisional IRA, and the animal liberation front. Now it's moved to fixated people and there are a lot of people fixated about Harry and Meghan and that raises the threat level.

‌



"I think Harry will continue to employ his own private security team, but in the hope that he can persuade RAVEC to upgrade in whatever shape or form. I think that's his hope now he's going to have a permanent address."

View 7 Images Harry and Meghan have reportedly already found a house and schools for their children in the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Harry, 41, now plans to continue to lobby RAVEC to complete an urgent review into his security, after he sent the department a report from his private security company claiming he is a terror target.

‌



He has made several trips back to Britain from his home in Montecito, California, but has been forced to pay for his own private security. A 40-page risk assessment suggested he faced an “elevated risk” in the UK, where five of the six known terror plots against him originated.

At least four individuals responsible for those threats are thought to be out of prison, and their whereabouts are unknown. The report, compiled at the request of the Home Office, said the biggest threat facing Prince Harry was from “lone actors” or “grassroots” terrorists, who often target public figures who receive high levels of negative publicity.

Harry was particularly angered that the government sent him the contact number for a liaison officer for him to call in an emergency, rather than respond to his request for the complete review.

‌



Last month, the Mirror revealed Prince Harry had been buoyed by an emotional reunion with the King and his family who were reunited in person for the first time in four years. Sources revealed Harry wants his father, who is suffering from cancer, to be able to spend more time with his grandchildren, who he he had hardly seen since the Duke and Duchess quit their royal roles in 2020 and moved to California.

View 7 Images Harry and Meghan pictured at the Invictus Games un The Hague in 2022 (Image: ANP/AFP via Getty Images)

Harry returned for events surrounding the one-year countdown to his Invictus Games being held in Birmingham next summer. But the duke’s hopes of engineering a meeting between his father and his family were initially dashed just 24 hours after revealing his full UK itinerary, which included Meghan joining him on stage at the Invictus event at Birmingham’s The National Exhibition Centre.

‌



He had planned to stay at Buckingham Palace with Meghan and their children, but the King pulled the accommodation suggesting his estranged son had not replied in time to organise suitable staffing to host them at the palace. At the time, sources suggested the Home Office was further angered by Harry’s plan, suggesting the duke announced his itinerary in the hope of forcing the government to grant them security which was removed when the Duke and Duchess left their royal roles in 2020.

After announcing plans to all travel to London together from a family holiday in Europe, the Sussexes were forced to travel separately when they received notice that the Home Office would not facilitate round the clock security for them for the visit.

Harry did eventually manage to arrange a meeting with the King at his Highgrove estate in Gloucestershire - alongside Queen Camilla - meaning Charles managed to spend precious time with his grandchildren for the first time since 2022.

Article continues below

Neither the palace or the Sussex's team have revealed details of the meeting, apart from the fact it took place on Saturday, July 11, where Charles and Camilla hosted them for afternoon tea. One source described the meeting as “emotional”.

News.title: Harry and Meghan's return to UK reignites questions over security
News.content:
In terms of why they were moving now, a source close to the couple said the "stars had aligned" at this time to make the move work for their family.

They are described by the source as an international couple who love to travel - and for the next while they are going to be based in the UK.

As well as surprising the world's media, it was also news to King Charles, who was told about the move on Sunday. He is said to be looking forward to seeing them more often.

The decision follows a visit in July by Prince Harry, Meghan and their children to see the King at his Highgrove home in Gloucestershire.

It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years, and the couple's first visit to the UK together since 2022.

It has also been two-and-a-half years since the King was diagnosed with cancer and in Prince Harry's BBC interview last year, he spoke of wanting to spend more time with his father.

Highgrove has the feel of a family home rather than a royal palace - and royal author Valentine Low says a key driver of their return has been the chance for Harry to rebuild links to his family and particularly to "repair his relationship with his father".

The couple will still keep their California home and Meghan's work in the media and her online food business, As Ever, can be carried out from a base in the UK as readily as in the US.

Next year, Prince Harry's Invictus Games are being held in Birmingham, which would have meant extensive travelling to meetings and events in the UK.

It will also mark the 30th anniversary of the death of his mother, Princess Diana, which will bring commemorations and events in the UK.

This summer saw Prince Harry and his family staying at the Spencer family home at Althorp and returning to the UK will be a chance to be closer to his mother's side of his family.

News.title: Watch: What does Harry's return mean for his fractured relationship with William?
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, and their children, are planning on relocating back to the UK from the US later this month.

Prince Harry and Meghan left the UK and stepped back from royal duties in 2020, and family relations have been strained since.

The BBC understands that whilst King Charles III welcomes their return, he wasn't informed of it until Sunday.

There has been no official comment from his brother, the Prince of Wales.

News.title: Five key takeaways from GCSE results day 2026
News.content:
You might be forgiven for glancing at this year's GCSE results and thinking not much has changed.

And sure, if you're just looking at the pass rate across England, Wales and Northern Ireland, that would be more or less correct.

But, when you dig into the detail, you'll find a more complicated picture, where some issues from last year have become even more stark.

You'll see the grades of students resitting their English and maths GCSEs in England are dragging down the overall results in those subjects - all part of a system the government itself says is "demoralising" and needs fixing.

You'll see that boys' and girls' grades are looking more similar - though that's more to do with girls slipping than boys improving.

And you'll see that, despite the government's pledges to "tackle entrenched inequality", the regional divide in England has actually grown, and remains stubbornly higher than it was before Covid.

Here are five key things you need to know.

News.title: Academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism suspended by university
News.content:
An academic who accused the late Cambridge professor Jason Arday of plagiarism has been suspended from his post at a Belgian university.

Nathan Cofnas, a self-defined "race realist", was among those to question Arday's work and achievements - prompting a weeks-long plagiarism row prior to his death on 14 August.

Cofnas said he was under investigation by Ghent University "for discriminating against Arday".

The university said a staff member had been notified of a "preliminary disciplinary investigation" and suspended as a precaution.

In a statement regarding Arday's death, its rector Petra De Sutter and vice-rector Herwig Reynaert said they took "recent public statements made by a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University regarding this matter very seriously", and had taken "appropriate action".

They said the university stood for "respect for human dignity and opposes discrimination, hatred and racism".

"We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited.

"It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others."

They said Arday's death should "prompt reflection" and that lessons should be learned "regarding the way we treat one another both within and outside the academic world, particularly when people become the subject of public controversy".

Cofnas works as a postdoctoral researcher at the university's department of philosophy and moral sciences, according to his website.

His role at a Cambridge college was terminated in 2024 after backlash to his view that, under a true meritocracy, black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

News.title: John Swinney defends £45,000 business-class flights to World Cup
News.content:
John Swinney has defended the use of more than Â£45,000 of public funds on business-class flights for him and two senior aides to the World Cup.

Scotland's first minister flew to Boston on 11 June for Scotland's opening match, before taking part in trade talks in Kentucky three days later.

While he and two senior officials travelled business class, Sports Minister Maree Todd and several other officials went to the US on significantly cheaper economy-class flights.

Swinney insisted the government had sought to "minimise" costs, while Justice Secretary Neil Gray defended the business class flights as a means of ensuring ministers "arrive fresh" when they travel overseas.

In total, the government spent Â£98,442 on trips for Swinney, Todd and their officials to the US, including flights, hotels and expenses.

Flights for Swinney and his private secretary John Webster cost Â£17,893 each.

Business-class tickets for the first minister's special adviser Colin McAllister cost Â£9,864.

News.title: Belgian car salesman becomes prince after royal parentage confirmed
News.content:
Belgium's Prince Laurent has legally recognised 26-year-old former car salesman ClÃ©ment Vandenkerckhove as his son and heir.

Vandenkerckhove, the result of a relationship between the royal and Belgian singer Wendy Van Wanten, was quietly brought into Prince Laurent's family at a town hall ceremony six months ago, although details have only just emerged.

While he formally becomes a prince, he will not receive a royal allowance.

The new prince has had several years to get used to the idea of having a royal father, and he said recently he was not yet sure he would begin using his father's name Saxe-Coburg.

"I might want to do that, but I am proud of the name Vandenkerckhove," he told Het Nieuwsblad.

"If I were to sacrifice that family name, it would be a betrayal of everything my mother has done for me."

He will not be part of Belgium's royal line of succession, unlike his half-sister Princess Louise and half-brothers Prince Aymeric and Prince Nicolas. Nor will he take part in public royal activities.

Vandenkerckhove is already well known to Belgians, having been the focus of a Flemish TV documentary last September, in which he described how he got to know his father.

His father had been in a relationship with Wendy Van Wanten, whose real name is Iris Vandenkerckhove, before he went on to marry Princess Claire in 2003.

During the VTM documentary, ClÃ©ment described meeting the prince unexpectedly in a shopping centre in 2013, without realising who he was. It was only when he was 16 that his mother revealed his father's identity.

Four years later he plucked up the courage to ring him up, and after several more calls they met in person and eventually Prince Laurent suggested they take a DNA test.

"We went to the hospital together and I remember him saying 'I'll go first so you're feeling at ease'," he told VTM. Then he received an email from the laboratory which told him of a 99.5% DNA match.

Prince Laurent's DNA test is reminiscent of his father, former King Albert II, who had a test after a lengthy paternity battle. Albert admitted in 2020 that he had fathered a daughter during an affair and eventually recognised her as his own.

Albert II abdicated as king of the Belgians in 2013 as the paternity issue became a royal scandal.

Delphine BoÃ«l, a well-known artist, eventually won her court battle and gained the right to the title of princess, and now calls herself Delphine de Saxe-Coburg.

Under changes to Belgian law in 2013, only a few members of the royal family are entitled to public allowances - King Philippe, his father King Albert II, Prince Laurent and Princess Astrid.

News.title: BBC DJ Trevor Nelson reveals brain tumour surgery 'went well'
News.content:
BBC DJ and presenter Trevor Nelson has revealed he stepped away from work after being diagnosed with a brain tumour.

Nelson was last on air in June and had announced he was "taking a little break from my work commitments" due to "health issues".

Speaking to his Instagram followers, external, the 62-year-old said that his "world was turned upside down" when a brain tumour was discovered.

He said that he had undergone a "very serious surgery" which "went incredibly well".

Speaking on Instagram on Thursday, Nelson explained: "There's been a lot of speculation as to what's wrong with me, I know that much. My phone's blown up 20 times over with people asking what's wrong with me.

"I felt that I should at least tell you what was wrong with me. I'm not going to go into it all now and I will deep dive into it at a later date so you can hear the full story."

He continued: "I'll tell you this, I was minding my own business and then it was discovered I had a brain tumour.

"I was shocked, my world was turned upside down, it was a shock to myself and close family and friends and you can imagine quite literally my head was all over the place."

News.title: Man charged over Manchester synagogue attack
News.content:
A man has been charged in connection with the Manchester synagogue attack in which two men were killed.

Counter terrorism police said Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, 49, of St James Road, Higher Broughton, Salford, had been charged with failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity.

Hakim has been remanded into custody to appear before Westminster Magistrates' Court on Friday.

There have so far been eight arrests in connection with the attack, however this is the first charge that "relates directly" to the morning of 2 October, when two men died as the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue was attacked by Jihad Al-Shamie. He was shot by police and died at the scene.

Worshippers Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, were killed.

Assistant Chief Constable Rob Potts, from Counter Terrorism Policing North West (CTPNW) , said: "This is a significant development in our investigation, and my thoughts are with all those affected by the attack, particularly the bereaved loved ones and survivors.

"We have updated them and continue to offer them as much support as possible.

"Since the attack took place, we have been unwavering in our commitment to establishing the full picture behind the incident and identifying anybody who may have been involved in any way."

In July, Mohammad Bashir, 31, who planned an attack on a military base with the Manchester synagogue attacker was jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years.

He drove his friend Jihad Al-Shamie on a 10-hour round trip to conduct hostile reconnaissance at the UK's Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, on 14 August 2025.

Weeks after that journey, Al-Shamie, 35, was shot dead by police after carrying out the Heaton Park Synagogue attack.

News.title: 'Relentless' GCSE resit cycle 'simply not working', school and college leaders say
News.content:
The "relentless" cycle of pupils in England failing and then resitting their GCSEs in maths and English is "simply not working", a leading education union has said.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) said a "significant proportion" of students fall short of passing those subjects, and that most who retake those exams "face the miserable experience of falling short once again".

Thursday's results data showed nearly one in four maths and English GCSEs in England were taken by students aged 17 and older, mostly young people resitting exams they had previously failed.

The government said it wanted to stop the "endless treadmill of unnecessary resits".

It said it would introduce a new "stepping stone" qualification from 2028 at Level 1 - one level below GCSEs - for students who do not achieve a pass in GCSE maths or English.

Currently, many courses and jobs remain dependent on students securing GCSE passes in those subjects.

But those that miss the grade can find themselves in a continuing loop of resits as they try and try again to pass.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of ASCL, said the fail-resit cycle was like "force feeding" students a "relentless diet of GCSE English and maths".

"This limits their education and career options and is very likely to be a factor in the large number of young people who end up not in employment, education or training," he said.

Pass rates for students aged 17 and older in English and maths are much lower than 16-year-old students taking the exams for the first time, bringing down overall GCSE grades for all ages across England, Wales and Northern Ireland as a result.

News.title: People smuggler exposed by BBC investigation arrested and charged
News.content:
A convicted people smuggler who was found by the BBC to be living in Leicestershire has been arrested and charged with immigration offences.

Twana Jamal Khdir, an Iraqi national who was once described as "the godfather" of the French migrant camps, previously served a sentence for people smuggling in France.

Last month, the BBC revealed he was now living in the UK.

The BBC has been told he was arrested on Tuesday near Uppingham in a joint operation led by the Midlands Criminal Financial Investigations team, with the support of Leicestershire Police.

He was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service and appeared at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

He pleaded guilty to entering the UK without valid entry clearance, but not guilty to seeking to obtain leave to enter or remain by deceptive means.

He has been remanded in custody and will next appear at Leicester Crown Court on 5 October.

Khdir was given a five-year jail sentence in France in 2016, where authorities described him as one of the most successful people smugglers ever caught.

Prosecutors said the Iraqi Kurd, aged 36 at the time, had earned up to Â£100,000 a week for moving illegal immigrants across the Channel.

News.title: Thunderstorm warnings expire but rain continues to bring risk of floods for UK
News.content:
Heavy showers and thunderstorms will continue to affect large swathes of the UK on Thursday afternoon, bringing the threat of flooding and travel disruption.

A Met Office yellow thunderstorm covering parts of northern England and north Wales expired at 13:00 BST, with focus of heavy downpours shifting southwards across England and Wales.

Drivers are still being warned that wet weather could lead to slippery conditions and flooded roads.

The Environment Agency has issued one flood warning, external for Walverdon Water in Nelson, Lancashire.

Temperatures are also dropping with some places expected to remain below the August average over the next few days.

News.title: Vapes could lead to health harms in children, doctors warn
News.content:
Vaping could lead to health harms in children and young people and should be made "less attractive" to them, doctors have said.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) has reviewed about 81 studies into vaping and said it is linked to higher rates of breathing problems and evidence of harm in babies whose mothers used vapes while pregnant.

The review said vaping should not be seen as a "harmless part of growing up".

The RCPCH is calling on the UK government to go further in its proposals to place new restrictions around the sale of vapes and suggests limiting the number of flavours that are available.

The review into vapes has been published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood. Experts from the college looked at the studies involving health or social outcomes of vaping on children and young people.

It said vaping had an association with problems including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

Co-author of the systematic review, Prof Will Carroll, said the evidence showed "clear links" with respiratory symptoms, nicotine dependence and subsequent cigarette smoking.

"We must act to make vaping less attractive and accessible to children," he said.

Vice-president for policy of the RCPCH, Dr Mike McKean, added: "Vaping is still a relatively new product, and there is much we do not yet know about its long-term impact on children and young people but a clear and concerning picture is emerging."

"We need to keep pace with a rapidly evolving market and continue to take action to protect children from nicotine products."

In July, the government launched a 12-week consultation on the appearance, packaging and display of vapes with the aim of reducing the appeal of the products to children.

As part of the new proposals, packs would need to be plain with strict limits on branding and only simple flavour descriptions like "apple" or "cola" used.

Other restrictions would move vapes out of sight in shops, similar to how cigarettes and tobacco are currently sold.

The 100-day consultation follows the recent passing of the Tobacco and Vapes Act,, external which sets out proposals to create the UK's first smoke-free generation.

Children aged 17 or younger now face a lifelong ban on buying cigarettes, since it will be illegal for shops to sell tobacco to anyone born after 1 January 2009.

Dr McKean said the new act was "an important step towards protecting children from nicotine addiction, but it must not be seen as a one-and-done solution".

Prof Carroll said the government needed "to go further and limit the types of flavours available to them as opposed to just their descriptions".

News.title: School 'deeply saddened' by death of family in sea off Shoreham
News.content:
A school attended by a 14-year-old girl who died alongside her father and mother after getting into difficulty in water off the coast of Shoreham-by-Sea has paid tribute to her.

Sara El-Khawas and her parents, husband and wife Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, are believed to have gone into the water near Shoreham Fort in West Sussex on Tuesday, according to Sussex Police.

In a statement on its website, the Ellen Wilkinson School for Girls in Ealing, west London, described Sara as a "sweet girl, well-liked by staff and students".

A fourth member of the family, a younger girl, remains in hospital in a critical condition, police confirmed on Thursday.

News.title: Burnham announces plans to clean up worst three illegal waste dumps
News.content:
Three of the country's worst illegal dumps are due to be cleaned up using taxpayers' money, the government has announced.

Sites in Kent, Surrey and West Yorkshire will be assessed for clearance, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying the "toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long".

Fines for waste offences will also rise from Â£300 to Â£5,000 to deter, catch, and punish those who dump illegally, and the Environment Agency will have more powers to seize assets bought with the proceeds of crime by those involved.

But opposition parties said illegal dumps were a small part of a much bigger issue with smaller scale fly-tipping and landfill all posing big problems for communities.

Burnham is looking to build on work started by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to tackle waste crime, with an action plan published in March detailing a series of measures - including using drones to map illegal waste sites.

Sir Keir's administration had announced that sites in Wigan, Sheffield and Lancashire would have government clean-ups - alongside Kidlington in Oxfordshire where removal of 20,000 tonnes of waste started in April.

The government said the new sites identified for clearance contain around 22,000 tonnes of illegally dumped waste.

They are: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road in Bradford, West Yorkshire.

West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester will be the first areas with new region-led approaches to waste crime.

The government said this will give mayors and council leaders the lead in co-ordinating councils, police, regulators, and other enforcement agencies.

Speaking on a visit to the waste dump in West Yorkshire, Burnham said: "We've begun a much more networked approach to this, where we're bringing the National Crime Agency in to work with the Environment Agency, increasing the penalties and bearing down now on the organised crime that lies behind some of what you see behind me."

The prime minister said the aim was to build intelligence about criminals linked to waste dumps at an earlier stage, to avoid the public being charged for clean-ups.

"We should be getting in much earlier, apprehending them, using all of the intelligence that comes through that investigation to make sure the polluter pays," he added.

A new "waste crime crackdown group", chaired by Environment Secretary Angela Eagle, will bring regulators and law enforcement together in a bid to dismantle criminal operations.

Eagle said: "We are cleaning up sites, but we are also stopping the cycle, driving faster prevention and disruption, better intelligence, and stronger coordination across the system."

News.title: Reform UK proposes tax rebates for firms to boost apprenticeships
News.content:
Young apprentices should have part of their wages paid by taxpayers, according to Reform UK plans, external aimed at delivering a "skills revolution".

The party's education spokeswoman Suella Braverman said a Reform government would introduce an "apprenticeship wage credit" offering small and medium-sized businesses a 30% rebate on the wages of apprentices they take on aged 16 to 18.

She also advised students receiving their GCSE exam results on Thursday "not to get ripped off by the great university scam" and to learn a trade instead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants teenagers to have technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a traditional university degree.

The government has been introducing changes and examining ways to encourage more young people into work, including giving some parents on benefits up to Â£4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships.

Former minister Alan Milburn has been tasked with investigating why so many young people are not in employment, education or training - known by the acronym Neets.

Reform said its announcement was the first in a series of proposals aimed at reaching 600,000 apprenticeship starts per year by the end of the next Parliament, likely to be 2034.

The party says it would pay for its plans by banning all foreign students from accessing taxpayer-funded loans and stopping what the party calls "Mickey Mouse degrees".

Reform said its policy, which also includes a Â£2,000 retention bonus for apprentices, could cost between Â£1.48bn and almost Â£2bn over five years.

Braverman said there are "excessive number of graduates with qualifications that don't match the skills needed for our country," arguing that learning a trade would be a better use of their time.

Apprentices are generally paid a lower wage but get on-the-job training and practical work experience.

Speaking at a press conference, Braverman said: "We're firing the starting gun on unleashing a technical and vocational renaissance of homegrown skills.

"Reform will not do this because it fills us with some jingoistic pride but because we will do what it takes to save Britain from the perpetual doom loop of decline, debt and despair that we're currently in."

The MP said the apprenticeship wage credit would result in businesses saving an average of Â£4,000-a-year per apprentice.

The Â£2,000 tax-free retention bonus would be paid to workers who "show loyalty" by staying with the business that trained them for at least two years after they complete their apprenticeship, said Braverman.

Asked if the policy would mean some universities would have to close, Braverman said she did not envisage that but instead suggested universities need to "repurpose" themselves into construction colleges and manufacturing colleges.

When pressed to give examples of "Mickey Mouse degrees", Braverman pointed to "gender studies" and "golf course studies".

She said: "There's not a necessity, there's not a value in many of these degrees."

The British and International Golf Greenkeepers Association (BIGGA) has previously criticised Braverman for similar remarks, which they branded "negligent and potentially damaging".

BIGGA chief executive Jim Croxton said: "Golf course management is a growing industry with currently more vacancies than qualified applicants.

"Anyone successfully studying for a degree in this field is effectively guaranteed employment in a vibrant industry."

A Labour Party spokesperson said all young people "deserve a clear route to a good career" whether through "a properly funded apprenticeship, high-quality technical education or university".

The spokesperson added: "That's exactly what this Labour government is already delivering, with 500,000 new jobs, apprenticeships and training opportunities to help young people earn or learn, including a guaranteed job for 18â24-year-olds who have been out of work for 18 months."

On Wednesday, Conservative shadow education secretary Laura Trott said there is demand for apprenticeships but claimed the Labour government "aren't doing enough to boost supply".

She said: "Our New Deal for Young People would axe the dead end degrees that don't lead to jobs and instead invest in apprenticeships giving school leavers more choice."

Liberal Democrat universities spokesperson Ian Sollom said it was important to protect local colleges and universities as well as boosting apprenticeships, including apprenticeships in degree courses.

"Reform's proposals amount to dangerous economic vandalism which would rip a multi-billion-pound hole in our world-leading university sector," he added.

Green Party MP Hannah Spencer, who was a plumber before becoming an MP, said: "People are tired of Reform pitting us against each other - Those of us that did apprenticeships can still see the value in degrees and everyone should be able to choose their own path of education."

She added the Greens had announced a windfall tax on big banks, which she said would support small businesses employing more young people.

News.title: Rare Suffragette Christmas card from 1910 found at roadshow
News.content:
A rare Suffragette Christmas card from around 1910 has been discovered at a vintage roadshow.

The card, found in Mold, Flintshire, and which comes from the height of the campaign to win women the vote, was produced to raise funds and awareness for the movement.

Today, surviving examples are "exceptionally scarce", according to antique shop WeBuyVintage, which has valued the item at Â£2,500.

"These weren't simply Christmas cards, they were pieces of political campaigning that helped fund one of the most significant social movements in British history," said Matt Case, an antiques specialist.

Case said that finding an original Suffragette Christmas card was "incredibly exciting".

Because they were intended to be seasonal and disposable, "very few have survived, especially in such good condition", he added.

Sold by organisations such as the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU), they helped finance the campaign while keeping the movement visible during the Christmas season.

Museums, including the London Museum, external, now hold examples in their permanent collections as important artefacts documenting the fight for women's voting rights.

In Wales, Lady Rhondda, born Margaret Haig-Thomas, led a 40-year campaign for women to be allowed to sit in the House of Lords - although she died just before the law she fought for was changed, too late to take her own seat.
