World.title: Western Romania: Special exhibition in Timișoara to include 69 works by Pablo Picasso
World.content:
69 works by Pablo Picasso from the collection of the Musée Picasso, Antibes, will be on display in Timișoara, between September 17, 2026, and January 17, 2027, in a special exhibition that inaugurates the new Art Encounters space.

The event, titled "Picasso en visite," will include 69 works – paintings, drawings, engravings, lithographs and ceramics.

The exhibition starts from a particular moment in the artist’s life and work.

“In 1946, Picasso received an invitation to work in the spaces of the Grimaldi Castle, at that time the museum of the region’s history and archaeology. The artist had long dreamed of a place where he could work on a different scale than his studio allowed him to. The light of the Mediterranean, the sea, Greek mythology and the atmosphere of southern France became fixed in his imagination during a period of extraordinary creative freedom,” the organizers said in the presentation of the event.

Tickets can be purchased online at bilete.artencounters.ro and through the Entertix platform. To ensure that the visit provides the necessary time and space to encounter the works and for their safety, access to the exhibition is available in time slots and with a limited number of visitors.

Rates:

Adults (18–64 years): RON 65 (Tuesday–Thursday) / 75 (Friday–Sunday)

Children (8–17 years): RON 20 / 25

Family (2 adults + 2 children): RON 150 / 175

Seniors (65+) and students (up to 26 years): RON 35 / 45

Private tour for 2 people: RON 500

Access is free for children under 8 (accompanied by an adult), people with disabilities or reduced mobility and their companions, press representatives and holders of AICA, ICOM and ICOMOS cards.

On the last Tuesday of each month, the exhibition can be visited free of charge, between 10:00 AM and 8:00 PM. Tickets for these days will be available that morning at the Art Encounters ticket office, subject to availability.

During the exhibition, guided tours will be available both in Romanian and in some foreign languages, with prior reservation. Art Encounters will also organize free visits dedicated to school groups, with details about the schedule and registration to be announced soon.

World.title: Romanian meat and ready-made meals processor Cris-Tim reports 34% higher net profit in H1
World.content:
Cris-Tim Family Holding (BVB: CFH), one of the largest players in Romania’s processed meat and ready-made meals market, reported revenues of RON 567.4 million for H1 2026, up 6%, and a net profit of RON 63.6 million, 34% higher compared to the previous year

According to the company, the results were supported by the continued growth of the processed meat segment, which advanced by 7% compared to the previous year.

The Cris-Tim brand remained the main pillar of the segment, generating revenues of RON 348.6 million, up 4% compared to the previous year. The Matache Măcelaru brand recorded revenues advancing by 24% compared to the previous year, to RON 77.8 million, reflecting growing consumer interest in traditional and premium products, as well as the brand’s expanding presence in modern retail networks.

The other brands in the Processed Meat portfolio generated RON 77.2 million, up 9% compared to the previous year, an evolution supported both by the positive dynamics of the company’s brands and by Private Label production. Segment EBITDA reached RON 93.4 million in H1 2026, representing an increase of 28% compared to 2025.

The Ready Meals segment generated revenues of RON 55.7 million in H1 2026, down 2% compared to the previous year, and accounted for approximately 10% of total revenues. Sales volumes decreased by 8% compared to the previous year, while the average selling price per ton increased by 7%, reflecting a more favorable product mix.

The Bunătăți brand generated revenues of RON 34.3 million in H1 2026, compared to RON 35.9 million in H1 2025, while the other brands in the Ready Meals portfolio advanced by 3% compared to the previous year, to RON 21.4 million, an evolution supported by the expanding presence in modern retail networks and the diversification of the product range. Despite the slight decline in segment revenues, Ready Meals EBITDA increased by 11% compared to the previous year, to RON 15.2 million, reflecting the improved sales mix and the stronger contribution of products with higher margins.

Overall EBITDA increased by 28% compared to the previous year, to RON 110.7 million in H1 2026, while the EBITDA margin increased by 3.4 percentage points, to 19.5%, compared to 16.1% in H1 2025.

“The improvement was mainly driven by the favorable procurement strategy, increased production efficiency and an improved product mix. Profit before tax increased by 41% compared to the previous year, to RON 79.8 million, while net profit reached RON 63.6 million, up 34% compared to the previous year, and the net profit margin improved to 11.2%, compared to 8.9% in H1 2025,” the company report stated.

“In just a few months, two of our newest products – Gratarescu and Durdulii, the latter launched under the Matache Măcelaru brand – have quickly become among consumers’ preferred choices in their respective categories,” said Radu Timiș Jr., CEO of Cris-Tim Family Holding, in his message to investors.

As of June 30, 2026, the company's cash position reached RON 139.1 million. Net debt stood at RON 116 million, compared to a net cash position of RON 5.6 million at the end of 2025, mainly reflecting the seasonal accumulation of inventories and investments made in the first half of the year, according to the company. The debt level remained moderate, with the annualized net debt-to-EBITDA ratio standing at 0.52x, and the net debt-to-equity ratio at 29.4%.

Following the H1 2026 results, which exceeded expectations, management updated the 2026 Income and Expenditure Budget. The updated budget reflects significantly higher profitability expectations, with EBITDA currently estimated to reach RON 238 million, approximately 14% above the initially approved budget, and gross profit at RON 173.9 million, approximately 19% above the initial target. The revised EBITDA margin is estimated to reach 19.8%, compared to 17.1% according to the initial budget.

World.title: British-Romanian Chamber of Commerce appoints Felicia Alexandru as Executive Director
World.content:
The British-Romanian Chamber of Commerce (BRCC) announced the appointment of Felicia Alexandru as Executive Director on Tuesday, August 18.

The appointment comes at a time of growing economic relations between the two countries. Bilateral trade in goods and services reached GBP 10.4 billion in the four quarters ending at the end of March 2026, up 5.6% compared to the previous similar period, according to the latest data from the UK Department for Business and Trade.

According to the BRCC press release, Felicia Alexandru’s priorities will include strengthening dialogue between Chamber members, institutions and authorities, developing the Chamber’s program of events and initiatives, and facilitating new opportunities for collaboration, investment and commercial development in the two markets, Romania and the UK.

“We are pleased to have Felicia join us at an important moment for the development of the BRCC and the economic relationship between Romania and the United Kingdom. Her experience in diplomacy, consulting and coordinating complex teams will support the implementation of the strategic direction established by the Board of Directors,” said Robert Uzună, President of the British-Romanian Chamber of Commerce.

“I take on this role with great confidence, at an excellent time for our trade ties. I am joining the valuable BRCC team with a clear desire to bring a new dynamic and to be close to every business leader. My priority is to listen to the needs of members and transform the remarkable expertise within our network into real projects,” said Felicia Alexandru.

Before joining the BRCC, Felicia Alexandru led the Romanian operations of Aperio Intelligence, a British risk management and business intelligence consultancy. Before this position, starting in 2021, she coordinated the company’s due diligence teams in Bucharest and Cluj-Napoca. Between 2008 and 2019, she worked at the British Embassy in Bucharest. Her experience was complemented by coordinating public integrity programs in the non-governmental sector.

Felicia Alexandru holds a degree in political science from the National University of Political Studies and Public Administration in Bucharest and a master’s degree in international relations and European studies from Central European University in Hungary.

(Photo source: brcconline.eu)

World.title: Romanian F-16 destroys maritime drone near Neptun Deep gas platform in the Black Sea
World.content:
A Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed a maritime drone near the Neptun Deep offshore gas platform in the Black Sea on Thursday, August 20, interim defense minister Radu Miruță announced. The operation was ordered to protect several hundred people working at the site and secure the critical infrastructure, he said.

According to minister Miruțǎ, the Coast Guard announced that the maritime drone was detected several hundred meters from work underway at Neptun Deep, in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, around 80 miles east of Constanța. The Defense Ministry later added that the drone was drifting when it was first reported by a commercial vessel at around 6:28 a.m.

“A maritime drone was destroyed by the Romanian Army using the onboard cannon of a Romanian F-16 aircraft a few moments ago, in the area of the Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea,” Radu Miruță wrote on Facebook on Thursday around noon.

A command cell was established at the Ministry of National Defense following the discovery. The ministry requested that NATO transfer operational command of the response to the Romanian military, according to the interim minister.

“Following the analyses carried out and in coordination with the president of Romania, the decision was made to destroy the drone in order to protect the lives of the several hundred people working on the platform and secure the critical infrastructure,” Miruță said.

Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets were scrambled with authorization to open fire. The maritime drone was subsequently destroyed without incident.

“The drone was destroyed safely,” the interim defense minister announced.

According to him, the Romanian authorities contacted Ukraine through a recently established direct communication channel and received official confirmation that the drone was not of Ukrainian origin.

According to the Defense Ministry, a Coast Guard ship carrying a Romanian Navy explosive ordnance disposal team was sent to the area to conduct further checks, while the operation remained ongoing.

President Nicușor Dan also reacted to the news, saying, "I congratulate the Romanian Armed Forces and the pilots of the two Romanian F-16 fighter jets on the successful mission to destroy the maritime drone near the Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea. I also congratulate the Coast Guard for promptly reporting the drone’s presence in the area. It was a race-against-time operation in which the highest priority was protecting the lives of those working on the platform and keeping critical infrastructure safe from any potential danger."

"I strongly condemn the intensification of these irresponsible incidents by the Russian Federation. We remain vigilant alongside our NATO allies to defend ourselves and repel such provocations," he added.

This was the first time Romanian aircraft used their onboard cannons and also the first time they engaged a maritime drone, Biziday.ro noted.

The incident came hours after an aerial drone entered Romanian airspace near Galați early on Thursday and crashed in an unpopulated area near Grindu, Tulcea County. Two Spanish F-18 aircraft and a Romanian IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter were deployed during that incident, while residents in the affected area received an RO-Alert warning.

Last week, two Gerbera-type drones were destroyed by divers of the Romanian Army in the exclusive economic zone, approximately 90 nautical miles (around 165 kilometers) from Constanța, in the Neptun Deep exploitation area.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Facebook/Radu Miruțǎ)

World.title: STRABAG PFS to enter Romanian market through acquisition of Brenneka companies
World.content:
STRABAG Property and Facility Services (STRABAG PFS), a subsidiary of the European construction group STRABAG, agreed to acquire 100% of Romanian companies Brenneka Install and Samivo Instal. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to approval from the relevant authorities.

The STRABAG subsidiary signed the acquisition agreement on August 11. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Both target companies are part of the Brenneka Group, which is headquartered in Bacău and has an operational office in Bucharest. The acquisition will mark STRABAG PFS’s entry into the Romanian market and expand its Building Solutions business in Eastern Europe.

Funded in 2007, Brenneka has more than 230 employees and provides installations for civil and industrial construction projects in Romania. Its services include heating, ventilation and air-conditioning systems, plumbing, electrical and automation systems, fire protection, municipal networks, design and engineering, as well as construction and fit-out work.

“Through the acquisition of Brenneka, we are […] entering a market with significant growth potential that is of strategic interest to us,” said Stefan Babsch, managing director of the STRABAG PFS Group.

“Brenneka benefits from a strong market position and extensive expertise in building services. We are therefore expanding our service portfolio and creating a foundation for the further development of our Building Solutions business in Romania and Southeastern Europe,” he added.

Brenneka founders Mihai Ojog and Lucian-Florentin Vultur said the company was ready for a new phase of development.

“Together with STRABAG PFS, we will combine the experience and expertise we have built over nearly 20 years with STRABAG’s resources, expertise, and international presence,” they said.

STRABAG PFS currently operates in Germany, Austria, Poland, the Czech Republic, and Luxembourg, providing technical and infrastructural facility management, building services engineering, property management, and industrial services.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Romanian energy authority ANRE approves mechanism to reward voluntary consumption reduction
World.content:
Households and companies in Romania could be financially rewarded if they agree to consume less electricity during certain periods, according to a new regulation approved by Romania’s energy authority ANRE, highlighted by Euronews Romania.

Following the change, during periods when the energy system is under pressure, energy grid operator Transelectrica will be able to establish how much consumption needs to be reduced and will organize an auction. Companies, suppliers, or other eligible participants will be able to say by how much they are willing to reduce their consumption and for what amount.

The mechanism would reward voluntary consumption reduction so as to balance the national energy system, under pressure after Romania’s sole nuclear energy plant shut down.

Until now, when the system needed more energy, the solutions were increasing production or imports. With the new mechanism, eligible consumers can be paid to temporarily reduce their consumption.

The reduction in consumption will be voluntary, and consumers, suppliers, or aggregators will be able to participate in the program. For example, if a factory would normally consume 10 MWh during a certain period, it could offer to reduce consumption by 2 MWh in exchange for a sum of money.

The mechanism could eventually also reach households. An energy supplier could bring together a large number of customers in such a program and reward them when they reduce their consumption during periods when the grid is under heavy strain.

For example, during a peak period, such as 7:00-8:00 PM, customers enrolled in the program could be asked to delay turning on the washing machine or boiler, reduce the use of air conditioning, or postpone charging certain equipment.

The savings made by a single household would be small, but if tens of thousands of consumers do this at the same time, the amount of energy saved can become significant for the system. Participating consumers could, in return, receive a bonus for the energy they did not consume during that period.

However, approval of the regulation does not mean that Romanians will automatically start receiving money for reducing their consumption. For the mechanism to reach household customers, suppliers or aggregators must participate in the program and also establish how the remuneration obtained for the energy saved will be transferred to consumers.

World.title: Illegal zoo in Romania’s Dâmbovița County shut down over animal mistreatment
World.content:
Romania’s National Environmental Guard announced that it closed an unauthorized wildlife facility in Dâmbovița County and issued fines totaling RON 220,000. The authority also filed a criminal complaint against the International Wildlife Foundation (IWF) after inspectors allegedly found animals kept in unsanitary and inadequate conditions, sometimes without food or water.

The facility operated as a so-called wildlife rehabilitation center but conducted activities specific to a zoo without an environmental permit, the Environmental Guard said.

Inspections carried out in July and September 2025 found four lions, a male tiger cub, and two brown bears for which the foundation could not provide documents proving their origin or the necessary CITES certificates.

Inspectors also reported that a male lion was kept without the minimum conditions required by law, while two tiger cubs were allowed to roam freely. A female baboon was allegedly displayed to visitors while restrained on a leash and lacked adequate space, food, and water.

“Today, we permanently closed an improvised center that kept wild animals in miserable and completely noncompliant conditions,” said Andrei Corlan, commissioner general of the National Environmental Guard.

“We removed a danger to the animals, which were kept in spaces that failed to meet minimum requirements and were often even without water and food, as well as a danger to people who happened to visit this completely illegal site,” he added.

The authority said IWF failed to comply with measures imposed after the July inspection by an August 13, 2025, deadline. It allegedly did not provide documents concerning the animals’ origin, the agreement governing use of the land, an emergency plan, or notification that the required measures had been implemented.

During the September inspection, officials found the body of one tiger cub concealed in a refrigerated container, according to the Environmental Guard. The second cub had allegedly been moved to a clinic without the authorities being notified, despite an order prohibiting the transfer of animals.

The fines included RON 60,000 for lacking the required permits, RON 60,000 for failing to provide appropriate living conditions, and RON 100,000 for missing the deadline to implement measures ordered by inspectors.

The Environmental Guard prohibited the collection from reopening to the public without an environmental permit and permanently banned the transfer or breeding of its animals.

The criminal complaint concerns suspected possession, transportation, or sale of specimens allegedly taken illegally from the wild.

The animals were assessed and microchipped by Romania’s veterinary authority, the Environmental Guard also said. Four lions and two bears were tranquilized with assistance from the Visul Luanei Foundation, while the two bears were transferred to the Zărnești sanctuary by the Millions of Friends Association.

World.title: Remains of 23 Wartime Victims Unearthed from Mass Graves in Kosovo
World.content:
Kosovo Police guards the mass grave location in Kalluder village on July 30, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

As forensic experts near the completion of weekslong excavations at three locations in the villages of Kalluder and Jabuke in northern Kosovo near Zubik Potok, authorities announced on Thursday that they have unearthed remains believed to belong to 23 individuals who have been missing since the 1998-99 war.

The identities of the victims will be determined following forensic examinations.

Acting Interior Minister Xhelal Svecla stated that the “remains of 23 individuals have been found in three mass grave locations”, believed to belong to Kosovo Albanian civilians who were forcibly disappeared during the war.

“Kosovo demands accountability about the masterminds, perpetrators, those who concealed the bodies, and those who hid information about the whereabouts of these bodies,” Svecla said.

“Serbia’s silence is concerning and this silence is open support for planners, organisers and perpetrators,” he added.

The excavations in Zubin Potok began on July 28.

Agron Limani, head of Kosovo’s Government Commission on Missing Persons, said the remains were found at three locations in the villages of Kalluder and Jabuke.

“The remains of 23 people have been found. So far, 20 have been exhumed and the final three are being recovered today. We hope the process will be concluded today,” Limani told BIRN on Thursday.

At the first site in Kalluder, the remains of 13 people were found and then transferred to the Institute of Forensic Medicine. The remains of four people were found at a site in Jabuke, while the remains of six were found at another location in Kalluder.

“The third location, in Kalluder, is around 300-400 metres from the first one. Six bodies have been found, three have been recovered and the remaining three are expected to be recovered today and transferred to Forensics,” Limani noted.

Kosovo’s Special Prosecution Office said on Wednesday that teams from the Institute of Forensic Medicine had identified skeletal remains believed to belong to at least 23 individuals.

“Full identification will be carried out after the completion of forensic examinations and the relevant procedures,” the prosecution said.

On July 29, acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti said that the authorities’ immediate suspicion upon locating the remains was that they could belong to a group of 23 intellectuals who disappeared during the war.

“Our immediate suspicion when we learned that mortal remains had been found was that it was the group of 23 intellectuals in Mitrovica who were kidnapped and forcibly disappeared. We must wait for our institutions to determine exactly what has been found there,” Kurti said.

Three individuals – J.R., M.J. and M.B. – are currently in detention in connection with the case on suspicion of committing war crimes against the civilian population.

A report published on July 29, 2026 by Kosovo’s Institute for Crimes Committed During the War notes that 1,578 people remain missing.

Kosovo authorities and families of missing persons have repeatedly called on Serbia to provide information and open its archives about the locations of burial sites of people forcibly disappeared during the war.

World.title: Montenegro Opposition Leader Claims PM Spajic is Serbian Army Reservist
World.content:
Montenegrin opposition leader Milan Knezevic on Thursday presented documents that he alleged show that Prime Minister Milojko Spajic sought to join Serbia’s military reserve and was subsequently accepted.

Knezevic called for Spajic’s resignation and questioned how a member of the Serbian armed forces could serve as prime minister of a NATO member state, Montenegro.

Knezevic, leader of the Democratic People’s Party, which until recently was part of the ruling parliamentary majority and which has close ties to Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, displayed three documents at a news conference in Podgorica.

He said the first showed Spajic applied on February 17, 2023 to become a member of the Serbian military reserve, while the other two allegedly confirmed his admission and obliged him to report for duty if required. The documents’ authenticity could not be independently verified.

Knezevic claimed the papers had been provided by “disappointed” members of Spajic’s Europe Now movement.

He accused the prime minister of violating several laws and deceiving the public.

Spajic responded to the allegations by accusing Knezevic of “obediently carrying out the tasks of his (in)formal boss from Belgrade” – a reference to Serbian leader Vucic – in an effort to slow Montenegro’s path towards the European Union.

“It is sad to watch a man who was indisputably rhetorically talented and interesting in the past,” Spajic wrote on X.

The allegations come amid a renewed dispute over Spajic’s ties to Serbia and his citizenship status.

In February 2023, Spajic’s candidacy for Montenegro’s presidential election was rejected by the State Election Commission after information emerged that he held Serbian citizenship and had maintained residence in Serbia.

Spajic said at the time that he had submitted a request to renounce his Serbian citizenship and had deregistered his Serbian residence.

His candidacy was ultimately rejected, and the Europe Now movement replaced him with Jakov Milatovic, who went on to win the presidential election.

Knezevic also alleged that Spajic had received political backing from Serbian President Vucic, before later turning against him.

Knezevic called on President Milatovic and EU ambassador Johan Sattler to address the allegations.

There was no public response from Serbian officials by the time of publication of this article.

World.title: Human Rights Watchdog Urges Italy, Albania to End Offshore Migrant Detention
World.content:
Italian police officers outside a fenced entrance at Gjader port in Albania, deployed as security for the arrival of migrants transferred by sea. Photo: BIRN/Nensi Bogdani.

The human rights organisation Amnesty International on Thursday called on Italy and Albania to end a deal designed to send migrants and asylum seekers to offshore detention in Albania.

In a new research report, Amnesty International said that the 2023 deal between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, “is jeopardising people’s safety, liberty and human rights”.

Under the scheme, adult males from countries designated as “safe“ who are intercepted by the Italian coastguard while attempting to cross the Mediterranean would be transferred by ship to detention centres in Albania, which are run under Italian jurisdiction. There, their asylum claims would be fast-tracked and completed within 28 days – far shorter than the months-long process typical in Italy – before likely repatriation.

“Offshore detention is ultimately aimed at deterrence and trying to shift and evade both the responsibilities of responding to people migrating and the obligation to provide asylum to those who need it. Italy’s deal with Albania shows yet again the unavoidable human rights costs of this approach,” said Eve Geddie, director of Amnesty International’s European Institutions Office, said in a press release.

“Just before the deal entered into force, Amnesty International sounded the alarm on the harmful impact it would inevitably have on the rights of people in distress at sea, and of people transferred to Albania. Clearly, these concerns have now materializsed,” Geddie’s statement added.

Italian courts ordered the first three groups that were sent to Albania be returned to Italy, citing an EU Court of Justice (CJEU) ruling from October 4, 2024, that a “safe country” designation must apply to the entire national territory.

In March 2025, Meloni abandoned the original plan pending a resolution of legal challenges. The Italian government then approved legislation instead allowing migrants and refugees issued with deportation orders from Italian authorities to be detained in Gjader, Albania.

The shift means that the Gjader camp has been converted into a repatriation centre for holding those who reached Italy, were rejected for asylum and then issued deportation orders.

According to Amnesty International’s research, 500 men have been “forcibly transferred to the Albanian detention centre in Gjader over the past 15 months.”

The report noted that “between 11 April and 16 May 2025, 42 critical incidents were recorded in the Gjader centre, including at least two attempted hangings, a protest where three people were injured from shattered glass, and various self-harm incidents.

“The Italian government has obstructed independent monitoring of the Agreement’s implementation, including by restricting parliamentary oversight and bypassing ordinary legislative processes. By limiting access and oversight by independent rights observers, what happens in the Albanian detention centres remains largely shrouded in secrecy,” the report said.

“Whilst people detained in Albania fall under Italian jurisdiction, their physical distance from Italy combined with limited access to lawyers, courts and other safeguards, significantly undermines the effectiveness of the right to seek asylum and to access justice,” the report added.

A BIRN investigation found that the cost of constructing the centres in Shengjin and Gjader almost doubled from 39.2 million euros to over 74 million, while the average cost per bed in Albania reached around 72,000 euros. The investigation also found that the entire procedure was conducted through direct negotiation and without competition.

World.title: Romania Destroys Drone Near Major Gas Project in the Black Sea
World.content:
The Romanian ‘King Ferdinand’ frigate off the coast of Constanta, August 2026. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT.

A Romanian F-16 fighter jet used its onboard cannon to destroy an explosive-laden maritime drone in the country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project, Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Thursday.

Miruta said Romanian officials had been alerted earlier on Thursday by the Coast Guard about a maritime drone spotted several hundred metres from the offshore facilities used for gas extraction at Neptun Deep, some 80 nautical miles east of Constanta, the country’s main city on the Black Sea coast.

“A command cell was established within the Defence Ministry, which requested that NATO assume command at the level of the Romanian Armed Forces. Following an assessment and in coordination with the president of Romania, a decision was made to destroy the drone in order to protect the lives of the several hundred people working on the platform and secure critical infrastructure,” the defence minister said.

“For the sake of speed, two Romanian F-16 fighter jets were scrambled with orders to fire. The drone was safely destroyed. It was carrying explosives,” Miruta added.

The minister said that, through a recently established direct communication channel with Ukrainian authorities, he had received official confirmation that the drone was not of Ukrainian origin.

President Nicusor Dan put the blame on Russia.

“I strongly condemn the intensification of these irresponsible incidents by the Russian Federation. We remain vigilant alongside our NATO allies to defend ourselves and repel such provocations,” Dan said in a post on X.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also said in a public statement that “an escalating campaign of threats is underway, unsettling our citizens and seeking to divide our Union. This is hybrid warfare.”

She added: “With the European Drone Defence Initiative and the Eastern Flank Watch, we are scaling up production in Europe to deliver capabilities Member States need. So we can respond to emerging threats with speed, unity and resolve.”

This is not the first time drones have been destroyed in Romania’s exclusive economic zone near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project. On August 11, Romanian army divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones that had been drifting in the Black Sea.

Neptun Deep, jointly developed by OMV Petrom and state-owned gas producer Romgaz, contains an estimated 100 billion cubic metres of recoverable natural gas across two offshore fields.

The project involves investments of around 4 billion euros and is expected to start production in 2027, producing approximately 8 billion cubic metres of gas annually and nearly doubling Romania’s domestic gas output, strengthening energy security in the European Union.

In recent weeks, Romania has been facing an increasing number of drone incursions following the intensification of Russian attacks on Ukrainian maritime facilities along the Danube, near the Romanian border. It has shot down four drones that violated its airspace.

Two NATO F-18 fighter jets were scrambled on Thursday morning after an unidentified drone entered the country’s airspace, according to the Defence Ministry. The drone flew 13 kilometres over Romanian territory before crashing in an uninhabited area, causing no casualties.

World.title: Albania’s Flamingo Movement Said ‘No’, Now It Needs the Courage to Say ‘Yes’
World.content:
You’ll often hear the song Seven Nation Army during the ongoing street protests in Tirana. Written by the White Stripes more than 20 years ago, the song has been taken apart and rebuilt by the Albanian protesters.

The familiar riff, which has been used by demonstrators and football fans around the world, turns into a techno beat. The original words fade away. And then, from the crowd: “Rama, jepe dorëheqjen!” Rama, resign!

It is loud and angry, joyful and powerful.

The reimagining of the song is an act of creative appropriation: taking something that already exists and making it into something else. That is what protest does. It takes public space back. It takes language back. It takes the feeling that nothing can change and turns it into a crowd insisting that something must.

World.title: Animated Film Telling Story of Bosnian Child Massacre Survivor Premiered
World.content:
Some of the crew of ‘Fahrudin’ film, with BIRN Bosnia and Herzegovina staff and Fahrudin Muminovic. Photo: BIRN.

The 20-minute film ‘Fahrudin’ received a standing ovation from the audience when it was screened for a cinema audience for the first time on Wednesday evening at the Sarajevo Film Festival.

The film tells the real-life story of what seven-year-old Fahrudin Muminovic experienced during the 1995 Srebrenica genocide.

As Bosnian Serb troops closed in, he and his father Mehmed hid in a war-ravaged village but were found and taken to an execution site in Orahovac. The boy survived, despite being wounded, but his father died. In the film, his cry for his slain father, coming from beneath a pile of bodies, momentarily causes the executioners to halt.

After the shooting, a van driver who witnessed what happened defied the troops and took the wounded boy away with him. The film shows the van carrying Fahrudin setting off into an uncertain future as volleys of gunfire echo in the darkness.

Director and screenwriter Alen Drljevic said that the film “combines documentary and animation, a form very close to childhood that can convey just how young Fahrudin was when he survived the horrors of the genocide”.

The film was produced by BIRN Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Srebrenica Memorial Centre, based on an idea by Denis Dzidic, the executive director of BIRN Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Ahead of the premiere, Dzidic said that the story of Fahrudin had previously been told by BIRN journalists in other formats, but that it was important to bring the horror of what he experienced to the screen as well.

“The story of Srebrenica is very often reduced to numbers. To a single word – genocide. We don’t talk about testimonies that much, we don’t delve into people’s human experiences,” Dzidic said.

World.title: Russian Despatch: Kremlin’s Policy Inertia Exposed by Zelensky’s Belgrade Visit
World.content:
Russia has spent this summer in a state of growing uncertainty over the future. President Vladimir Putin remains determined to carry on with the war against Ukraine until reaching whatever he considers to be a victory, but most of the ruling elites and wider society are increasingly anxious about the absence of a clear exit strategy amid the lack of meaningful successes on the battlefield.

Their anxiety is further fuelled by Ukraine’s intensifying strikes against Russian oil refineries and online retail warehouses. The resulting gasoline shortages and bankrupting of small businesses is causing many Russians to experience firsthand the mounting costs of the war.

The mood shift in the Russia-Ukraine war has also been felt in the Balkans, where Kyiv has scored a major public relations victory. On August 8, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was hosted in Belgrade by his Serbian counterpart Aleksandar Vucic, despite the latter being widely perceived as Moscow’s most faithful ally in Europe. Officially, the two leaders met to discuss energy cooperation and humanitarian assistance, but it was arms deals that were on everybody’s minds.

Vucic publicly invited Zelensky to attend the upcoming opening of Serbia’s new drone production facility, constructed in cooperation with Israel. Simultaneously, leaks to the German press suggested that Serbia and Ukraine have gone as far as to plan the joint production of drones in Serbia to boost Kyiv’s military efforts.

World.title: ‘Room for All’? LGBT Pride Caravan Meets with Hostility in Smalltown Serbia
World.content:
In mid-July, LGBTQ+ activists in Serbia headed for the southeastern town of Pirot, on the second leg of this year’s Pride Caravan to raise awareness about LGBTQ+ issues and protest still widespread discrimination.

It was a good two-hour drive from Vranje, where their first event passed without incident despite threats posted in advance on social media.

The Caravan never made it into Pirot, however. On the town’s outskirts they were stopped by police, who warned them that opponents of the event were waiting for them on the central Warriors’ Square.

“The police told me ‘Well, we can’t arrest anyone. These are peaceful citizens; they’re not doing anything,’” recalled Matija Stefanovic, programme coordinator of Da se zna! [Let it be known], the organisation that runs the Caravan, an event designed to take the message of Belgrade Pride to smaller towns and cities in Serbia.

“Of course, it turned out that these were not peaceful citizens at all, but hooligans who physically attacked the male and female journalists who had arrived before us to cover our gathering.”

World.title: Conference League Play-Offs: Hajduk and Raków Draw 2-2 at Poljud
World.content:
Hajduk took on Raków tonight at Poljud in the first leg of the Conference League play-off round. Gonzalo Garcia’s side are two matches away from securing a spot in the group phase of the European competition, with the return leg set for next Thursday in Częstochowa at 7 pm.

Hajduk’s opponent is anything but easy, and virtually everyone in Split is well aware of that. It has been a staggering 16 years since Hajduk last enjoyed a European autumn campaign, and in that time the club has never been closer to a return to continental football. That is precisely why tonight’s match, for which Poljud saw demand outstrip ticket availability, carried such significance.

Lineups

Hajduk: Silic – Sigur, Maresic, Raci, Hrgovic – Pukstas, Pajaziti – Bamba, Dalisson, Soticek – Sego

Rakow: Trelowski – Tudor, Racovitan, Svarnas – Ameyaw, Kochergin, Repka, Ouma – Diaby-Fadiga, Emreli, Kwiatkowski

Match report

The match kicked off in a fantastic atmosphere at packed Poljud, with Hajduk chasing a place in the Conference League. It got off to a lively start — in the 4th minute, Bamba intercepted a pass from the visitors’ defense and burst into the penalty area, where he was impeded by Svarnas. Referee Očenaš waved play on, though, much to the loud disapproval of the home crowd.

In the 11th minute came the first real moment of danger at the Hajduk end. Ameyaw whipped in a cross, but Emreli caught goalkeeper Toni Silić in the head instead of the ball. The Split shot-stopper needed treatment as a result.

In the 17th minute, Bamba broke away down the left, using his pace to full effect before whipping in a low, first-time cross for Šego, whose effort was blocked, leaving Hajduk with a corner. The hosts worked it quickly from the resulting set piece in the 18th minute, with a well-rehearsed routine picking out Dalisson, though his shot lacked precision.

Hajduk deservedly took the lead in the 21st minute. Bamba delivered a cross for Šego, who timed his run to perfection, arrived unmarked at the far post and calmly nodded home to send Poljud into raptures!

Hajduk continued to press aggressively across every line in the 26th minute, which brought them another corner — again worked towards Dalisson, but once more the Spaniard’s effort lacked.

Raków levelled almost out of nothing in the 27th minute. Otieno powered past everyone down the left, crossed for Emreli, who nodded it home past Silić. It was 1-1.

In the 31st minute, Bamba — putting in an excellent performance, a constant threat and already with an assist to his name — won a yellow card for Otieno, the visitors’ provider for their goal. Two minutes later, Šimun Hrgović also picked up a booking for a foul from behind on the opposite side of the pitch. The impression is that the referee is reaching for early cards in an attempt to keep the players calm and maintain control and authority over the match.

In the 40th minute came a big scramble in front of the Hajduk goal, as Raków showcased their biggest weapon — set pieces. They whipped a delivery into the heart of the penalty area, but the resulting effort was blocked by one of their own players. Hajduk had a chance from a dead ball themselves in the 42nd minute, winning a free kick some 20 meters from the visitors’ goal — a big opportunity for Šego to add another set-piece goal to his tally.

The first half at Poljud came to a close in the 45+3rd minute. Hajduk have been much the better side on the pitch, going at Raków aggressively from the very first minute and keeping up that intensity right up until the whistle. Still, the biggest chance of the half fell to the visitors, in the closing stages, when Ameyaw’s effort came back off the post.

The second half got underway at Poljud, with the visitors making one change to start the period — Svarnas made way for Debohi.

Hajduk restored their lead in the 47th minute. Šotiček found Dalisson on the edge of the box, and the Spaniard, who had already enjoyed an excellent first half, fired home from 16 meters to send Poljud into another frenzy!

Hajduk went straight on the offensive at the start of the second half. Almost immediately from the restart, in the 48th minute, visiting goalkeeper Trelowski’s pass went straight to Bamba, who fired from around 30 meters, but his effort went wide of the post. Practically from the very next attack, Dalisson was left unmarked on a rebound and blazed his effort over the bar — complete pressure and offensive intent from Hajduk at the start of the half.

Hajduk’s afternoon took a turn for the worse in the 55th minute, however, when Pajaziti committed a heavy foul just around the halfway line. Referee Očenaš didn’t hesitate, showing him a straight red card. Hajduk will have to see out the rest of the match with ten men.

In the 65th minute, the visitors worked an opening for Pienko, but his effort was comfortably dealt with by Silić. Hajduk made a triple change in the 68th minute: Bamba was replaced by Šutalo, while Dalisson, scorer of the second goal, also made way, with Dario Melnjak coming on in his place. Slightly earlier, Gonzalo Garcia had already replaced Šotiček with Del Moral, who took over Pajaziti’s role on the pitch.

In the 72nd minute, Šutalo tried his luck from a half-chance on the counter, but his effort went over the crossbar. During the buildup to that move, the referee had played advantage following a foul on Melnjak, but then failed to book the offending visiting player once the phase of play was over — much to the frustration of the Split supporters.

In the 76th minute, Šego, scorer of the first goal, made way, along with Hrgović, with Marko Livaja and Alec van Hoorenbeeck coming on in their place. Tempers flared on the pitch in the 81st minute after the referee failed to award a foul by Pienko in midfield. Marešić reacted furiously towards Pienko in the aftermath, and it was ultimately the visiting player who ended up picking up a yellow card for the incident.

In the 82nd minute, Livaja let fly from around 20 meters towards the near corner, though Trelowski, not entirely without difficulty, managed to tame the shot. Pienko then tested Silić with an awkward header in the 90th minute, but the Hajduk goalkeeper made a confident save, gathering the ball safely into his grasp. Five minutes of stoppage time were added, and all Hajduk had to do was hold on.

But then the inevitable happened. In the 90+5th minute, Hajduk suffered a last-gasp blow. Once again, the Split side conceded deep into stoppage time to hand Raków a share of the spoils. The game ended 2-2 and the second leg is played in one week.

World.title: Croatia No Longer Near European Bottom in Terms of Annual Leave Affordability
World.content:
August the 20th, 2026 – Croatia is no longer near the European bottom in terms of annual leave affordability, but there are still serious issues with the overall standard of living.

At first glance the figure does not speak in favour of the standard of living in Croatia, however, the picture changes significantly when a longer period is looked at instead of a single year. This was pointed out by economist Ivica Brkljača and reported on by Edita Vlahovic Zuvela.

Almost a third of Croatian citizens over the age of 16 could not afford a week of annual leave outside their place of residence last year. According to the latest Eurostat data, 32.6 percent of the population were in this situation in 2025, placing Croatia seventh among European Union member states with the highest share of citizens for whom such a holiday is not financially accessible.

At first glance, this is a figure that does not speak in favour of the standard of living in Croatia. However, the picture changes significantly when a longer period is considered instead of a single year. Economic analyst Ivica Brkljača draws attention to precisely this, arguing that the 2025 figure should not be viewed in isolation. “The problem arises when this figure is observed in isolation, without the trend that shows how the affordability of annual leave has changed during the period of economic growth,” Brkljača stresses.

recession and recovery

In Croatia, this trend is particularly pronounced. In 2015 as many as 65.8 percent of the population could not afford a week of holiday away from home. Ten years later that share has almost halved, to 32.6 percent. This is an improvement of as much as 33.2 percentage points – the largest among all EU member states. For comparison, Cyprus follows with a drop of 25.9 percentage points, Ireland with 21.6, Bulgaria with 21.3 and Poland with 19.5 percentage points. Croatia’s position relative to the European average has also improved. In 2015 Croatia was the second-worst EU member state, right after Romania. The share of citizens who could not afford annual leave was then a full 30.6 percentage points higher than the EU average, Brkljača recalls. Last year Croatia was the seventh-worst EU member according to this indicator, while the gap to the European average has narrowed to 5.1 percentage points.

a lack of benefit equality

The biggest problem remains among the elderly and single people. Last year as many as 62.6 percent of people over 65 could not afford a week of holiday.

At the level of the entire European Union long-term progress is also visible. In 2015, 35.2 percent of the population could not afford a week of holiday away from home, while last year that share stood at 27.5 percent. Over ten years the share decreased in as many as 23 of the 27 member states, while increases were recorded only by Austria, Germany, Finland and Sweden. The enormous progress that has taken place in Croatia is further illustrated by Brkljača with data available since 2010, the first year for which figures exist for Croatia. The most difficult situation was in 2012, when as many as 71.4 percent of the population could not afford a week of holiday away from home. Very high shares persisted in the following years as well, and then, in parallel with the end of the prolonged recession and the start of economic recovery, almost continuous improvement followed.

Particularly interesting is the movement among households with dependent children. In 2012 as many as 71.3 percent of people from such households could not afford a week of holiday, and in 2015 the figure was 64 percent. Last year their share fell to 24.2 percent. Ten years ago almost two-thirds of such households could not finance a week of holiday, while today the figure is about a quarter.

croatia hasn’t yet reached the sort of living standard it should aspire to

One of the reasons for such pronounced improvement is probably the fact that it mainly concerns the working-age population, which has more directly felt the strong growth in employment and wages. However, economic growth has not affected all groups equally strongly. The biggest problem remains among the elderly and single people. Last year as many as 62.6 percent of people over 65 who live alone could not afford a week of holiday. Among women living alone that share was 57.9 percent, and among men 45 percent.

The number of children in the household is also not unimportant. Around 15 percent of households with one or two children cannot afford a week of holiday, while among those with three or more children the share rises to 33.1 percent. “The growth of GDP, wages and pensions has certainly been felt in the mentioned indicator, as well as in other indicators of the material position of households,” Brkljača concludes. This does not, of course, mean that Croatia has reached the level of living standard it should aspire to. But the trend is hard to ignore: over the past ten years Croatia has achieved the largest reduction in the share of the population that cannot afford a week of holiday among all EU member states.

prices and cost of living are the major determinants

Data from a survey conducted by Alma Career Croatia, the company that runs the MojPosao/MyJob portal, shows a somewhat more cautious picture for this year – more and more employees are planning shorter holidays, and the share of those who will not travel at all this summer is also rising. The share of employees who plan to use a maximum of seven days of annual leave has increased from 15 to 21 percent, while the share of those planning to rest for 21 days or longer has almost halved – from seven to only three percent.

The biggest change concerns those who do not plan to travel at all this summer. Their share has risen from 27 to 32 percent. In other words, almost every third respondent will not go on a summer holiday, primarily because of money. Among those who do not plan to travel, as many as 60 percent cite lack of money as the main reason, compared with 56 percent a year earlier.

Long-term Eurostat data also shows some major progress: the possibility of affording a week of holiday is significantly greater today than ten or fifteen years ago. However, the current survey of employees shows that prices and the cost of living still strongly determine how citizens will spend the summer. Croatia has therefore taken a big step forward, but the benefits of economic growth are not equally distributed. For some pensioners, single people and larger families, a holiday away from home remains a cost that is difficult to fit into the household budget.

World.title: Beijing and Zagreb Connected by a Frequent Airline for the First Time
World.content:
August the 20th, 2026 – Beijing and Zagreb are now connected by a frequent airline for the first time, and tickets are already on sale.

Sinisa Malus writes for Poslovni that China is ready to launch its new route between Beijing and Zagreb via Bucharest on 4 September, which will be the first regular air connection between China and Croatia. Speaking at an event at the Romanian Embassy in Beijing, the president of China National Aviation Holding, Cui Xiaofeng, said that the new route “will further strengthen and enrich Air China’s network in the Central and Eastern European market,” while at the same time establishing a more convenient air bridge for trade, economic cooperation, cultural ties and people-to-people exchanges between China and Croatia.

tickets are already on sale

Air China announced that the route is part of its strategy to deepen its presence in Central and Eastern Europe and further expand its international network, reports Ex-Yu Aviation News. The Chinese carrier also commented on the three-hour stop in Bucharest, noting that the relatively long wait will allow passengers continuing to Zagreb to complete passport control formalities there, meaning they will not have to do so upon arrival in the Croatian capital. Air China plans to operate year-round services between the three cities and has already put tickets on sale for the 2027 summer season.

Dario Mihelin, croatian Ambassador to China

I’m convinced that this flight will make it easier for Chinese tourists to travel to Europe, not only to Croatia but also to neighbouring countries. Passengers can book tickets exclusively between Bucharest and Zagreb, although prices on that sector will vary depending on the number of connecting passengers. Chinese tour operators have already started selling tourist packages for Croatia that include the new flights. During the upcoming winter season, Air China will offer 34,980 seats on its routes to Zagreb. Croatian Ambassador to China Dario Mihelin stressed that this is truly a historic moment for Croatia, as China and Croatia, or rather the capitals Beijing and Zagreb, will for the first time be connected by a regular year-round air route.

an opportunity for not only croatia but the immediate region

“I’m sure that without the coronavirus pandemic, this flight would certainly have been launched much earlier, given that almost half a million Chinese visitors already came to Croatia in 2019. That same year we were already discussing a feasibility study for this flight with representatives of a number of airlines, including Air China,” Mihelin said.

The ambassador added that this route will contribute to better people-to-people connections, strengthening not only tourism cooperation but also economic relations and trade between Croatia and China. “I’m of the belief that this flight will make it easier for Chinese tourists to travel to Europe, not only to Croatia but also to neighbouring countries, such as Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro,” Mihelin concluded.

World.title: Zagreb Invests Over 3 Million Euros in Tram Track Renovation
World.content:
August the 20th, 2026 – As Zagreb invests over 3 million euros in tram track renovation, it seems that work to get them completed quickly will see boots on the ground at night, at weekends and even on holidays.

Poslovni reports that the procurement procedure also includes four stationary devices for lubricating tram rails, including their delivery, installation, commissioning and functional testing. For the repair of tram tracks, the City plans to allocate 3.1 million euros. A public procurement is being prepared for works on tram infrastructure, ranging from the replacement of damaged concrete elements and cover plates to the arrangement of tracks and surfaces along the rails. The work would be ordered successively over two years, depending on the condition of the tracks and needs on the ground.

The City of Zagreb plans to conclude a framework agreement with several economic operators, and when the need for a specific intervention is established, the contractor will receive a written request. Work must then begin no later than within 36 hours, and individual contracts may last up to 12 months.

The City is conducting the procedure for ZET, and the documentation provides for the possibility of carrying out works during the day, but also at night, from 22:00-06:00, with slowed or completely suspended tram traffic. Contractors must be prepared to work on weekends and holidays as well, while works may take place simultaneously at a maximum of three locations.

According to the bill of quantities, there will be no shortage of work. Planned, among other things, is the dismantling of around 2,800 reinforced concrete cover plates, while 3,300 are planned to be installed. The removal of 2,500 concrete elements and the installation of 2,000 new ones is also envisaged. The works include the renovation of elements along the rails, their fastening and levelling, after which the track will again be closed with reinforced concrete plates, asphalt concrete or crushed stone, Večernji list reports.

The interventions also cover surfaces between and along the rails. The removal of a total of 2,200 square metres of the existing base layer is planned, as well as the asphalting of 2,000 square metres of roadway surfaces and an additional 100 square metres of pedestrian surfaces. On sections of the tracks where the track is closed with concrete and asphalt, the removal of around 500 cubic metres of existing fill and the construction of a new one is planned. Works will also be carried out on the crushed-stone base and track fill, in a total quantity of 200 cubic metres.

The procurement also includes four stationary devices for lubricating tram rails, including their delivery, installation, commissioning and functional testing. The City notes that the quantities in the bill of quantities are indicative, so the actual quantities executed, as well as the final cost, may be higher or lower than planned.

It should also be recalled that works are currently entering the final phase at the intersection of Savska and Vukovarska streets, one of Zagreb’s busiest junctions. Since the beginning of July, tram switches and crossings have been being replaced there, and according to the City’s latest available data, the asphalt wearing course has been completed on the greater part of the intersection.

At the same time, a major reconstruction of the tram track in Zvonimirova Street is underway. According to the latest status from the construction site, all earthworks have been completed, around 50 percent of the new rails have been laid, and the concreting of the reinforced concrete slab is currently being carried out. This will be followed by backfilling with crushed stone and the continuation of laying the new track. In addition to the main section of Zvonimirova, works are also being carried out at the intersection with Šubićeva Street, where the reconstruction of the worn-out track structure, including the replacement of a tram switch, began in mid-July.

World.title: Omiš Donation Account Published as Help Arrives From All Sides
World.content:
August the 20th, 2026 – A special Omiš donation account has had its details published as help arrives from across Croatia.

Poslovni reports that around ten residential containers have already been sent to Omiš, and companies are also offering to donate finished housing units. Damage assessment has begun in the Omiš area after the catastrophic fire that left devastation from Lokva Rogoznica to Omiš. Around 50 houses burned down, just as many were damaged, and a long recovery lies ahead for the residents. In addition to the consequences of the fire, landslides and rockfalls now also pose a threat.

Burned land, destroyed houses, hospitality facilities and cars are the scenes that greet residents and services on the ground. HEP workers are being helped by numerous volunteers in restoring infrastructure, and part of the area still has no electricity. An additional problem lies with the now unstable rocks and terrain without vegetation. During the night rocks fell twice in the Borko area, and two Civil Protection teams from Zagreb are using drones to inspect the rock mass above Omiš and Lokva Rogoznica, HRT reports.

expert assessments

Deputy Mayor of Omiš Ivan Pivčević said that experts will specifically check the protective nets above the town, installed about ten years ago, to determine whether they were damaged in the fire and extreme heat. Particular attention is being paid to the Borkavanje area, known for landslides. Experts from Zagreb will also be involved in the assessment to determine how unstable the terrain is now and what risk heavier rains could pose. Over 90 completely or partially damaged buildings have already been recorded, and tomorrow 20 experts organised into ten teams will go out into the field. They will assess the structural integrity of the houses and determine which buildings residents can safely return to.

the special Omiš donation account

Omiš has published on its Facebook pages the details and account number for donations and assistance for the remediation of the consequences of the fire and help for those affected in the area of the City of Omiš. “The City of Omiš would like to extend its sincere thanks to all natural and legal persons, units of local and regional self-government and other donors for the solidarity and help shown,” they said.

World.title: Quiet Inheritance: Why the Croatian Diaspora Should Seek Citizenship For Their Children
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Even if you don’t plan to open a business, move, or do anything concrete, as a member of the Croatian diaspora, gaining citizenship could mean the gateway to EU education and career opportunities for generations to come.

For a growing number of American parents who happen to have Croatian ancestry, the decision to pursue Croatian citizenship is no longer mainly about their own travel plans or personal connection to the country. It’s about their children…

eu citizenship is about so much more than getting through the border more quickly…

Across the United States, parents are quietly assembling birth certificates and family records. Maybe they were fuelled by the sense of sweeping national pride the World Cup brought, or maybe the fact that that burdensome double taxation treaty between the USA and Croatia is on its way to being scrapped. Maybe it’s none of that. It could be a desire to reconnect with the roots of their ancestors as a nod to all they went through for better lives across the Atlantic Ocean.

Whatever the reason behind the move, the end goal of such a move is relatively straightforward – to secure Croatian citizenship. Even if there are zero plans to move to Croatia or anywhere else in the EU, start up a business, move a company to the EU or retire, holding Croatian (and thus EU) citizenship means that their sons and daughters can also do the same, automatically gaining full EU rights. That of course includes unfettered access to higher education and unrestricted work opportunities across 27 different countries.

This isn’t just another theoretical benefit. Once a parent becomes a Croatian citizen through descent, minor children can typically acquire the same citizenship with far less complexity involved. That single step creates a permanent legal pathway that remains open for the next generation, regardless of whether the family ever relocates.

a european education with zero barriers

One of the clearest practical advantages is university access. EU citizens generally pay the same tuition rates as local students at public universities throughout most of the European Union. In many countries those fees are substantially lower than the costs American students face at home, and in some cases they approach zero for EU nationals. Holding a Croatian passport also removes the need for student visas or complex sponsorship arrangements when applying to programmes in Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Ireland, or other member states. Students can move freely for short courses, semester exchanges, or full degree programmes. The Erasmus network and similar mobility schemes become far more accessible when the student already holds EU citizenship rather than relying on temporary permissions.

For families watching American college costs rise astronomically year after year, this represents a concrete parallel option. It doesn’t require abandoning American universities. It simply expands the menu of realistic choices available to a teenager who holds both an American and a Croatian passport. It is also far easier on the pockets of parents who may only just be making ends meet.

career mobility following graduation – eu wide

The advantages continue after university is over and those famous photos are taken with diplomas in hand. An EU citizen can accept a job offer in any member state without needing a work permit or employer sponsorship. That flexibility matters in competitive fields where companies increasingly recruit across borders. Young dual citizens can take internships in Zagreb or just across the border in Ljubljana, accept graduate roles in Berlin or Amsterdam, or return home to the United States with the knowledge that EU opportunities remain permanently available to them whenever they get the itch to experience them.

Parents who secure the status of Croatian citizens while their children are still minors effectively hand them a form of professional insurance that is extremely difficult to obtain later in life. Rules can (and do) change. You only need to ask the Italian diaspora about the hurdles they now face in what was once an easy ride in getting Italian citizenship. Documentation becomes harder to locate and do anything with as older relatives pass away and time marches on. Completing the process now removes those future variables entirely and ensures flexibility that can hardly be matched in any other manner.

multi-generational safety

Many American parents with Croatian heritage say they have no intention of moving to Europe themselves. Nor do they need to. That’s totally irrelevant to the value of having Croatian citizenship for the next generation. The rights exist whether or not anyone relocates anywhere else. A family can remain fully based in the United States while still giving their children the legal ability to study, work, or live anywhere in the EU if they later choose to do so.

The same logic applies to grandchildren. Citizenship acquired today can, at least under current rules, be transmitted further down the line, creating a multi-generational safety net that requires just one single successful application at the starting point.

timing matters…

The administrative process for Croatian citizenship by descent is (in)famously document-heavy. Birth, marriage, and death records must be gathered, apostilled, and translated… The list goes on. That goes without even mentioning that much older records from the former Yugoslavia or earlier periods can take time to locate and deal with administratively. Consular and ministry processing times currently range from several months to well over a year depending on the complexity of the file.

Parents who begin while their own parents or grandparents are still able to help locate family documents often find the process smoother. Waiting until a child is already applying to universities can leave too little time for the citizenship to be finalised. For American families with verifiable Croatian ancestry, the window remains totally open. There is (at least for now) still no generational cutoff for eligible descendants in most descent-based cases, and dual citizenship with the United States is entirely permitted. The practical question is simply whether the family wants those EU education and mobility rights locked in for the next generation while the paperwork is still manageable.

The decision is less about returning to Croatia, less about business and investments, and more about giving children a permanent set of options that most of their American peers will never have. In an era of rising education costs and increasingly mobile careers, that quiet inheritance is proving more valuable than many families initially expected.

how croatianbydescent.com can help you get your hands on that trusty little blue passport

Croatian by Descent helps the diaspora to take that first step into the (sometimes choppy) waters of gaining Croatian citizenship. It acts as a complete guide to everything you might need to keep in mind when applying or just seeking more information. For total beginners with little to no knowledge of how administrative processes work in Croatia, this can be an invaluable source of guidance throughout the entire process.

Booking a free consultation with Croatian by Descent can set you on the path to securing Croatian and EU citizenship for yourself, thus making travelling to Croatia and Schengen for holidays easy and stress-free. It can also be a priceless gift to your children and grandchildren should they decide to take the leap (even temporarily) back to the country your ancestors left long ago, to attend higher education or to work, opening up a world of incredible opportunities that aren’t on the table for everyone.

World.title: Business Owners and Landlords Seek Relief After Fire in Omiš
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Business owners and private landlords are seeking relief and compensation after the fire that has ravaged the Omiš area.

The well known association Glas poduzetnika (UGP – Voice of Entrepreneurs) has proposed that the Croatian Government adopt an emergency package of measures that would temporarily relieve entrepreneurs affected by the fire in the Omiš area of tax, tourism, chamber and local charges.

Poslovni reports that the association believes that assistance must not be limited only to those whose facilities physically burned down, because damage in the affected area is also suffered by those whose facilities remained intact but who, because of the fire, were left without guests, access, income or the possibility of regular business operations.

“Such a package of assistance should not have to be reinvented every time. Croatia needs a predefined model of automatic relief and assistance to the economy in the event of fires, floods, earthquakes and other major disasters. When a catastrophe occurs, entrepreneurs must know what they can expect, and the state what it must do – without months of waiting for special decisions,” states UGP, which joined the request for urgent assistance at the initiative of the association Spasimo male obiteljske iznajmljivače – SMOi (Let’s Save Small Family Landlords).

They, for their part, are demanding exemption from payment of tax and other charges at least until the end of 2026, while for 2027 they are asking that the need to continue these measures be reassessed according to the actual situation and the speed of recovery of the affected area, noting that “one cannot expect a family from whom the fire has taken the season and income to continue paying the state as if nothing had happened.”

It should also be added that the Zagreb City Administration has announced that Zagreb will donate 130 thousand euros in aid to Omiš.

World.title: Extreme Weather Inflicts Damage on Croatian Tourism and Agriculture
World.content:
August the 19th, 2026 – Extreme weather is damaging Croatian tourism and agriculture, with temperatures above 30 degrees lasting more than a month, the economic cost amounts to around one percent of GDP.

Extreme heat is becoming an increasingly significant economic risk, and Croatia could be among the more exposed European countries due to the structure of its economy. In addition to the usual summer heat, summer is the season in which temperatures are rising the fastest, the State Hydrometeorological Institute (DHMZ) revealed. Poslovni reports that from 1961 to 2020, the average summer temperature increased by between 0.3 and 0.6°C per decade, depending on the area.

In the same period, a significant increase was recorded in the number of warm days – days with a maximum daily temperature of at least 25°C – locally by up to 8.3 days per decade. “Climate change therefore does not simply mean less or more rain, but changes the timing, frequency and intensity of precipitation, and with it the associated risks,” DHMZ said. According to empirical findings for 35 countries, every additional degree above 30°C reduces labour productivity by around three percent.

risks to businesses

For companies, extreme weather conditions are no longer just a matter of meteorology or public health, but an increasingly concrete business risk. Extreme heat for some employers means fewer working hours, lower productivity, higher costs, pressure on agricultural yields and growing costs of adapting to new weather conditions. Heat thus becomes a risk that, unlike damage after a flood or storm, is often not immediately visible.

“Extreme heat creates significant business costs for European companies. According to relevant analyses, the share of lost working hours due to heat stress could rise from 1.4 percent in 1995 to 2.2–2.5 percent by 2030. According to empirical findings for 35 countries, every additional degree above 30°C reduces labour productivity by around three percent (1.3 dollars in purchasing power parity per hour of work). Among European economies, the largest drop in productivity is estimated for France, Italy and Slovenia, and Croatia does not deviate much from that trio.

In the short term, the largest part of the cost is borne by companies because wages do not decrease despite the drop in productivity, which reduces profit margins. An additional negative effect comes from warmer nights, which in 2024 caused a record 8.7 percent more lost sleep, further worsening the productivity of office workers as well,” said Hrvoje Stojić, chief economist at the Croatian Employers’ Association (HUP).

Stojić points out that in general the estimates hold that in the case of 30 or more days with temperatures above 30 degrees Celsius, the economic cost amounts to around one percent of GDP.

“What is particularly worrying is the fact that climate risks are no longer the exception, which is why they are increasingly becoming part of regular business planning. Every day of production interruption, logistics disruption or reduced employee productivity due to extreme conditions represents a direct financial cost,” said Marija Šćulac, vice-president of the Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK). “Croatia is among the countries that are particularly exposed to climate risks, especially due to the size of its economy and the structure of the economy.

According to World Bank estimates from 2025, Croatia will need additional investments amounting to around 1.1 percent of GDP annually for successful adaptation to climate change and decarbonisation, while it is emphasised that delaying adaptation will be more expensive in the long run than timely investments. That is why we now view climate change as a matter of managing business risks,” she added. Šćulac says that the sectors most exposed to higher costs due to high temperatures are those that depend on natural conditions or are energy-intensive. Agriculture is already facing the consequences of droughts and heavy rainfall that directly reduce yields.

This is also confirmed by data from the Ministry of Agriculture. The Strategic Study for the Agriculture Strategy states that high temperatures, droughts and large amounts of precipitation negatively affect agricultural production. In addition, when maximum daily temperatures above 30°C last for more than ten consecutive days, agricultural crops enter a state of heat stress and stop growing.

In agriculture, climate risk is first seen in yields, but for Croatia its broader economic consequences could be significantly greater in tourism. According to the European Commission Report for Croatia, the direct contribution to GDP is 11.8 percent, the highest among member states, while tourism-related sectors generate around a quarter of gross value added.

risks to tourism

“Due to high temperatures, guests are changing their habits and we can expect fewer of them to come during the hottest summer months. This means that the tourism sector will have to adapt its business models to the new climate circumstances and year-round tourism. Major challenges also await the construction sector, which must find a way to organise work on construction sites during extreme heat, while logistics and transport are already feeling the consequences of disruptions caused by droughts and low water levels,” Šćulac said.

8.7 percent is what the decline in productivity stood at back in 2024 due to warmer nights. Such a development could be particularly important for Croatia, whose tourism is strongly concentrated in the summer months. The European Environment Agency warns that climate change may affect the seasonality and geographical distribution of tourist demand also because of the growing risk of extreme heat.

“Paradoxically, the sector that is key to the transition is itself highly vulnerable. The energy sector is under pressure because droughts reduce hydropower production precisely when consumption is highest. That is why it is important to develop a balanced energy mix that includes renewable sources, but also – and this is crucial – a strong and modern electricity grid that will be able to accommodate an ever-increasing number of renewable energy sources. Since extreme weather conditions affect almost all sectors, the focus is on how ready each individual sector is to manage climate risks. Companies that invest in energy efficiency, digitalisation, their own renewable energy sources and resilient infrastructure will in the long run be more competitive than those that postpone adaptation,” Šćulac said.

Examples of the impact on logistics can be found everywhere, and the Dutch one stands out in particular because the Port of Rotterdam, as the largest and one of the most important, connects maritime traffic with river, rail and road transport and enables the distribution of goods in Europe. Cargo ships transporting chemicals, oil and other goods to and from Rotterdam can, due to low water levels, be loaded only to about 30 percent of capacity in order to prevent grounding, the Financial Times reported. This means that carriers have to pay for around 100 additional river cargo ships (barges) per week, yet still cannot transport the full quantity of goods as before the drought.

The World Bank in its 2025 report for Croatia estimates that, without additional action, climate events covered by their model alone could reduce Croatian GDP by up to 2.1 percent by 2050, with infrastructure, tourism and agriculture being particularly affected.
